sections.title: Set colors

sections.body:
Pie and donut charts draw the first series, one slice per category. The legend lists the categories, and selecting one hides its slice. The other slices then share the whole circle.

- **Data labels:** set `dataLabels` to print the percentage of each slice on it. Slices too narrow for the text show none.
- **Total:** set `totalLabel` on a donut to show the total in its hole, such as "Total". The total is the sum of the visible slices, unless you set `total`.
- **Colors:** slices use the palette in order, or `colors`. In HTML, each cell carries its slice color in `data-ok-color`.
sections.title: Show parts of a whole

sections.body:
Radial bar charts draw one ring per category on a grey track. Values are percentages: a ring is full at 100, or at `yMax` when you set it. Values print with a percent sign unless you set `valueSuffix`.

- **Gauges:** with one category, the center shows the value and the category name. Set `startAngle` and `endAngle` in degrees, clockwise from 12 o'clock. For example, -90 and 90 draw a semicircle.
- **Dashes:** `dashArray` splits the ring into dashes of that length in pixels. `trackWidth` sets the thickness of the track as a percentage of the ring (50 by default).
- **Total:** with several rings, `totalLabel` shows a total in the center. It is the average of the rings, unless you set `total`.
- **Fill:** rings fade from a lighter tone of their color. Set `fill` to `solid` for a single color.
sections.title: Show progress as rings and gauges

sections.body:
Some charts need several values for each point. In React, pass them as an array in `y`. In HTML, give each value its own column under a second header row. The series header spans its columns, and each value header names its part in `data-ok-part`.

- **Box plots:** five values per category: the minimum, the first quartile, the median, the third quartile and the maximum (`min`, `q1`, `median`, `q3`, `max`). `boxUpperColor` and `boxLowerColor` color the boxes above and below the median.
- **Range areas:** a low and a high value (`low`, `high`). Add a `line` series for an average.
- **Bubbles:** a value and a size (`y`, `z`). In React, pass `[x, y, size]`. The area of a bubble follows its size.

The tooltip lists every value, and screen readers read each cell with its series and part, such as "Scores, Q1".
sections.title: Show ranges and distributions

sections.body:
Heatmaps and treemaps draw each value as a cell in the color of its series. A larger value gets a stronger shade, so the colors still follow the theme. Selecting a cell, or moving to it with the arrow keys, shows its value.

- **Heatmaps:** one row per series and one column per category, such as metrics over time. The first series is the bottom row.
- **Treemaps:** one group per series, with one rectangle per category sized by its value. Each series lists its own categories: in React, give each point an `x` name. In HTML, write one row per category and leave the cells of the other series empty. Names print in the cells that fit them.
sections.title: Show values as cells

sections.body:
- **Funnels:** `funnel` draws the first series as bars centered on one axis, each as long as its share of the largest value, such as the stages of a sign-up flow. For a pyramid, order the values from the smallest to the largest. `barHeight` sets the thickness (80% by default).
- **Slopes:** `slope` joins each series' values across a few categories, usually two, such as before and after. The values print beside the first and last points, and the scale fits the data.
sections.title: Show stages and changes

sections.body: Set `sparkline` (`data-ok-sparkline` in HTML) to draw a chart without axes, grid or legend, such as a trend in a dashboard card or a table cell. A sparkline fills its container: give the container a height, or set `height` for the least height (40px by default). The tooltip, the keyboard and the data table still work.
sections.title: Fit charts in cards and table cells

sections.body:
Charts redraw only what changed, so they can follow live data, such as requests per second.

- **React:** pass new `series` and `categories` arrays. To keep a sliding window, drop the oldest points yourself.
- **HTML:** call `updateSeries(series, categories)` to replace the data, or `appendData([{ data: [value] }], { categories: [label], limit })` to add points to each series in order. `limit` keeps the last points only. The runtime rewrites the data table to match, so screen readers read the same values.

Updates keep the hidden series and the category under the pointer or the keyboard, so the tooltip shows the new value.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { getRuntime } from "@owlky/html";

  const chart = getRuntime().get(document.querySelector("#requests"), "chart");
  // Add the newest value and keep the last 12.
  function onData(time, requests) {
    chart.appendData([{ data: [requests] }], { categories: [time], limit: 12 });
  }
</script>
sections.title: Update data live

sections.body:
Set `zoom` (`data-ok-zoom` in HTML) to let people zoom into the x axis of line, area, column, scatter, candlestick and other charts drawn from left to right. The value axis keeps its scale, so values stay comparable while you move.

- **Mouse:** drag across the plot to zoom to that range. Hold Ctrl (or ⌘ on a Mac) and use the wheel to zoom around the pointer. A plain wheel still scrolls the page.
- **Touch:** pinch with two fingers. On a zoomed chart, drag with one finger to pan. A tap still shows the tooltip.
- **Keyboard:** `+` and `-` zoom, Shift with the Left or Right arrow pans, `0` resets. Escape hides the tooltip first, then resets the zoom.

Set `toolbar` (`data-ok-toolbar`) to add buttons for zooming in and out, resetting, panning with the mouse, and downloading the chart as SVG, PNG or CSV. Downloads start only when someone selects a button or presses a key, and a failure is announced to screen readers. In React, `zoomRange` and `onZoomRangeChange(range, reason)` control the zoom. A zoom that reaches the newest point keeps following new points, so a live dashboard stays on its latest data.
sections.title: Zoom, pan and export

sections.body: Give charts the same `group` (`data-ok-group` in HTML) to synchronize them, such as requests, errors and latency of one service. Moving the pointer or the keyboard over one chart shows the same category in all of them, and zooming one zooms the others. Synchronized charts should share their categories.
sections.title: Synchronize charts

sections.body: A brush chart is a small overview that zooms another chart. Give the main chart an `id`, then set `brushTarget` (`data-ok-brush-target` in HTML) on the overview to that id. Drag across the overview to select a range, drag the selection to move it, or drag its handles to resize it. The keys of a zoomable chart work on the overview too. The selection follows the main chart when it zooms by itself.
sections.title: Brush a chart

sections.body:
Annotations mark a moment, a range, a threshold or a point, such as a deploy or an incident. In React, pass `annotations`. In HTML, list them after the data table in `ul[data-ok-chart-annotations]`, one `li` each, with its label as text.

- **`x`:** a vertical line at a category, a date or a number, or a band up to `x2`.
- **`y`:** a horizontal line at a value, or a band up to `y2`.
- **`point`:** a marker at `x` and `y`.

Each annotation takes a `color` (`info` by default). The list stays readable by screen readers once the chart is drawn.
sections.title: Annotate charts

sections.body:
- **Candlesticks:** `candlestick` takes four values per point in `y`: open, high, low and close. Rising candles use `candleUpColor` (`success` by default), falling ones `candleDownColor` (`error`). Add a `line` series for an average.
- **Range bars:** `rangeBar` takes a start and an end value per point, such as the fastest and slowest response of a service. Set `horizontal` to draw them from left to right.
- **Timelines:** `timeline` draws tasks from their start date to their end date, one row per task. Give each point a text `x` (the task) and two dates in `y`. The axis shows minutes, hours, days, months or years, depending on the span.

In the data table, each value gets its own column under a second header row, such as Open, High, Low and Close.
sections.title: Show prices, ranges and plans

sections.body:
A stock chart is a candlestick, line, area or column chart of prices over time, with technical indicators, panes and a navigator. The first series is the price. Give each point a volume in `v`, such as `{ y: [open, high, low, close], v: 1200000 }`. In HTML, the volume is a column of the price series under the header `data-ok-part="volume"`.

Set `indicators` to compute indicators from the price. Each indicator is a type and optional parameters:

- **Overlays,** drawn over the price: `sma` and `ema` (moving averages, `period`), `bollinger` (`period`, `stdDev`), `vwap`, `donchian` (`period`) and `keltner` (`period`, `atrPeriod`, `multiplier`).
- **Oscillators,** each in a pane of its own under the price: `volume`, `rsi` (`period`), `macd` (`fastPeriod`, `slowPeriod`, `signalPeriod`), `stochastic` (`period`, `signalPeriod`), `atr`, `cci` (`period`) and `pvt`.

In HTML, list the indicators in `data-ok-indicators`, separated by semicolons. Write the type, then its numbers in the order above, then an optional color, such as `"sma 20 warning; rsi 14"`.

The panes share the date axis, so a zoom applies to all of them. The price axis fits the visible dates. `paneHeight` sets the height of each pane in pixels (120 by default). Set `navigator` to add a small line of the whole price under the chart. Drag the window on it to move through time, or drag its edges to show more or fewer dates. The navigator also turns on the zoom keys, so the keyboard reaches every date.

The tooltip is one readout of the active date in every pane: open, high, low, close, volume and each indicator. The legend shows and hides each indicator. The data table lists every computed value in its own column (`th[data-ok-indicator]`), so screen readers reach them too. In HTML, the runtime writes those columns. It never reads them back as data.
sections.title: Show stock prices with indicators

sections.body:
A Sankey chart shows how a quantity flows from sources to destinations, such as energy from its sources to its uses. Set `type` to `sankey` and describe the links instead of series:

- **React:** pass `edges`, one `{ source, target, value }` per link, with node ids as `source` and `target`. Pass `nodes` (`{ id, title, color }`) to name and color the nodes. Nodes without a color take `colors` in order, then the chart palette.
- **HTML:** write one table row per link: the source as the row header, then the target and the value. Mark the three column headers with `data-ok-part="source"`, `"target"` and `"y"`. When a node's id differs from its name, put the id in `data-ok-value`. Put a node's color in `data-ok-color` on its cells.

The chart places each node in a column by its distance from the sources, sizes it by the larger of what flows in and out, and moves nodes to reduce crossings. A link that goes back to an earlier column, such as recycled material, is drawn as a dashed loop under the chart.

- **`orientation`:** `horizontal` (the default) or `vertical`, which suits flows with many stages on a phone.
- **`nodeWidth`:** the thickness of the nodes in pixels (20 by default).
- **`whitespace`:** the share of the fullest column left between its nodes (0.18 by default).
- **`fill`:** `gradient` (the default) fades each link from the source color to the target color. `solid` uses the source color, or the link's own `color`.
- **`edgeOpacity`:** the opacity of the links (0.4 by default).
- **`axisTitles`:** a title above each column, such as years in an alluvial chart. In HTML, separate the titles with semicolons in `data-ok-axis-titles`.
- **`dataLabels`:** adds each node's value after its name.

Point at a node to highlight its links and see what flows in and out. Point at a link to see its source, target and value. The keyboard moves through the nodes and links column by column. Names that don't fit between two columns are shortened with an ellipsis, or left out on narrow screens. The tooltip and the data table keep the whole name.
sections.title: Show flows between stages

sections.body: Set `animations` (`data-ok-animations` in HTML) to grow the series in when the chart first draws, and to move bars, points and lines to their new values when the data changes. Animations never play when the system asks for reduced motion. Live charts that update often read better without them.
sections.title: Animate charts

sections.body: `locale` formats numbers and month names. The names of the values in tables and tooltips, such as Minimum or Open, come from the second header row of the HTML table. In React, pass them in `localeText`, together with the toolbar's button names and the download error. In HTML, call `setLocaleText(text)` on the instance for the toolbar.
sections.title: Localize texts

sections.body: Set `dataLabels` (`data-ok-data-labels` in HTML) to print values on the chart: percentages on pie and donut slices, values inside columns and bars, and values above the points of lines, areas and radars. A label is left out where it doesn't fit, such as on a short column. The tooltip and the data table still show every value. Set `dataLabelBackground` to put the labels above points on a badge, which keeps them readable over lines. For your own text, pass `dataLabelFormatter(value, series, index)` in React, or call `setFormatters({ dataLabel })` on the HTML instance. Pie and donut labels get the percentage.
sections.title: Print values on the chart

sections.body:
Set `stacked` to put the series of a category on top of each other, so the column shows their total. Without it, columns of several series stand side by side. Only the end of each column is rounded.

- **Shares:** set `stackType="100%"` (`data-ok-stack-type="100%"` in HTML) to stack each category's values as shares of their total. The value axis runs to 100%, and data labels print the shares. The tooltip and the data table keep the values.
- **Totals:** set `stackTotals` (`data-ok-stack-totals`) to print the total of each stack past its end. Negative stacks get their total below.
- **Bars only:** in a mixed chart, set `stackOnlyBar` (`data-ok-stack-only-bar`) to stack the bar series and keep a line, such as a target, on its own values.
sections.title: Stack and compare series

sections.body:
Bars take options of their own:

- **Label position:** `dataLabelPosition` (`data-ok-data-label-position`) puts data labels by the value end (`top`), in the middle (`center`, the default) or by the base (`bottom`) of each bar.
- **Value ranges:** `colorRanges` colors each bar by the range that holds its value, such as red for losses and green for profits. A point's own `color` wins. In HTML, write the ranges as text: `data-ok-color-ranges="-100 -1 error Loss; 0 100 success Profit"`.
- **Tracks:** `backgroundBars` (`data-ok-background-bars`) draws a grey track the height of the plot behind each bar, which helps when values are parts of a fixed maximum. `backgroundBarColors` (`data-ok-background-bar-colors`, palette names separated by spaces) colors the tracks category by category, `backgroundBarOpacity` sets their opacity from 0 to 1, and `backgroundBarRadius` their corner radius in pixels.

Color alone shouldn't carry the meaning of a range: name the ranges in the label or the text around the chart, as the data table only holds the values.
sections.title: Style bars

sections.body:
Some people can't tell the series of a chart apart by color, and printed charts often lose it. Give series a second cue, so color is never the only way to read the chart:

- **Marker shapes:** `markerShape` (`data-ok-marker-shape`) sets the shape of every marker: `circle`, `square`, `triangle`, `diamond`, `cross`, `plus` or `star`. A series can set its own `markerShape`. In HTML, write it on the series' column header. Lines draw markers only with `markerSize`, and scatter points always.
- **Patterns:** `fill="pattern"` fills bars, areas and pie, donut and polar area slices with a pattern, a different one per series or slice. `fillPattern` (`data-ok-fill-pattern`) picks one for all of them: `slantedLines`, `squares`, `circles`, `horizontalLines` or `verticalLines`. A series can set its own `fillPattern`.
- **Dashes and widths:** `dashArray` and `strokeWidth` set the dash length and line width of every line in pixels. A series can set its own `dashArray` and `strokeWidth` (`data-ok-dash-array` and `data-ok-stroke-width` on its column header).
- **All at once:** `colorBlindMode` (`data-ok-color-blind-mode`) gives each series its own marker shape, pattern and dash, and adds markers to lines.

The legend and the tooltip repeat each series' shape or pattern on its marker. To call out single points, such as a record, pass `discreteMarkers`: `{ seriesIndex, dataPointIndex, color, size, shape }` objects in React, or text such as `data-ok-discrete-markers="0 4 error star 8"` in HTML. They draw a marker on that point even when its series has none.
sections.title: Tell series apart without color

sections.body: `valuePrefix` and `valueSuffix` add text around every value, such as a currency or a percent sign. `locale` sets the number format and the month names. `yMin` and `yMax` fix the value axis, and `yTitle` names it. For anything else, pass `valueFormatter(value, series)` and `labelFormatter(x)` in React, or call `setFormatters({ value, label })` on the HTML instance. The axis gets `series` -1.
sections.title: Format values and axes

sections.body:
Pass `yaxis` to set up the value axis, or a list of axes to draw series of different units on one chart, such as visits and mentions. In HTML, write the axes in `data-ok-yaxis`, separated by semicolons, and mark each series' column header with the index of its axis in `data-ok-y-axis`.

- **`seriesName`:** the series drawn on this axis, by name. A series that no axis names goes to the axis at its own position.
- **`opposite`:** draws the axis on the right of the plot (`opposite` in HTML).
- **`logarithmic` and `logBase`:** a logarithmic scale for values that grow by factors, such as downloads. Ticks sit at whole powers of the base (10 by default). Values of zero and below aren't drawn, and series on the axis don't stack.
- **`reversed`:** the highest value at the bottom, such as a ranking where 1 is best.
- **`tickAmount`:** the number of intervals between ticks (`tick-amount` in HTML). Other axes take the number of intervals of the first axis, so their labels line up with its grid lines.
- **`min`, `max`, `title` and `show`:** fix the range, name the axis, or hide its labels while its series keep its scale (`min`, `max`, `title` and `hidden` in HTML, with the title last).

Several axes work on charts drawn from left to right with an x axis. `xTitle` (`data-ok-x-title` in HTML) names the x axis under its labels, and is also the header of the data table's first column unless you set `xLabel`.
sections.title: Add value axes and change their scale

sections.body:
By default, the tooltip lists the values of every series in the category under the pointer or the keyboard. Change it with these options:

- **One value:** `tooltip="point"` (`data-ok-tooltip="point"` in HTML) shows only the column, bar or point under the pointer, and the arrow keys move value by value.
- **No tooltip:** `tooltip="none"` shows no tooltip. Screen readers still announce the values the keyboard moves to, because the tooltip stays as a hidden status region.
- **Fixed position:** `tooltipFixed` (`data-ok-tooltip-fixed`) keeps the tooltip in a corner of the plot, so it never covers the values: `topLeft`, `topRight`, `bottomLeft` or `bottomRight`.

To show your own content, pass `tooltipContent(context)` in React. It gets the `title`, the `rows` (`name`, `value` and `color` of each value), `selected` and the data `points`, and returns what the tooltip shows. In HTML, add a `<template data-ok-chart-tooltip>` to the chart. The chart copies it into the tooltip and writes text into its slots: `data-ok-chart-tooltip-slot="title"`, `"state"` (removed unless the value is selected), and `"row"`, which is repeated for each value with its `"name"`, `"value"` and `"marker"`. The slots only ever get text, so data can't inject markup.
sections.title: Change the tooltip

sections.body:
People can select a value to act on it, such as opening the orders of one weekday. A click selects the column, bar, slice, cell or point under the pointer, and a second click clears it. With the keyboard, Enter or Space selects the item the tooltip shows. On a category with several series, it selects the value of every series. A selected value gets an outline in the text color, and its tooltip says **Selected**, so screen readers announce it too.

By default, a new selection replaces the previous one. Set `allowMultipleDataPointsSelection` (`data-ok-allow-multiple-data-points-selection` in HTML) to let selections add up.

- **React:** `onDataPointSelection(detail)` is called with `seriesIndex`, `dataPointIndex`, `selected` and `selectedDataPoints`. Pass `selectedDataPoints` to control the selection, or `defaultSelectedDataPoints` to start with one.
- **HTML:** `ok:chart:select` fires with the same `detail`. The instance has `selectedDataPoints`, `setSelectedDataPoints(list)` and `toggleDataPointSelection(seriesIndex, dataPointIndex)`.

`dataPointIndex` is the category's index, or the slice's in pie and donut charts. On numeric axes, it is the point's position in its series. A drag that zooms or pans selects nothing, and brush charts don't select.
sections.title: Select data points

sections.body: The legend shows one button per series, or one per category in pie, donut and radial bar charts. Selecting a button hides its series and fits the axis to the series that are left. Select it again to show the series. `legend` places the legend at the `top` (the default), `right` or `bottom`, or hides it with `none`. Charts with one series have no legend, unless you set `showForSingleSeries`. On screens narrower than 600px, a right legend moves below the chart. Set `legendValues` to show each item's value next to its name: the slice or ring value, or the last value of a series. `donutSize` sets the size of a donut's hole in percent of its radius (72 by default).
sections.title: Use the legend

sections.body:
Change how the legend looks and works:

- **Alignment:** `legendAlign` (`data-ok-legend-align`) lines the items up on the `left`, in the `center` or on the `right`.
- **Names:** `customLegendItems` shows these names instead of the series names. The first name stands for the first series, with its color and its button. In HTML, separate the names with semicolons in `data-ok-custom-legend-items`.
- **Fixed series:** `disableLegendToggle` (`data-ok-disable-legend-toggle`) turns the items into labels, for charts whose series must always show.

The grid draws horizontal lines along the value ticks by default. `grid` (`data-ok-grid`) draws `x` (vertical) lines, `both` or `none`. Stripes make rows or columns easier to follow: `gridRowColors` and `gridColumnColors` take colors in turn, such as palette names, `grey` or `transparent` (in HTML, separated by spaces in `data-ok-grid-row-colors` and `data-ok-grid-column-colors`). `gridRowOpacity` and `gridColumnOpacity` set their opacity, 0.5 by default.
sections.title: Customize the legend and the grid

sections.body: A chart fills the width of its container and redraws when that width changes, so text keeps its size. `height` sets the height of the plot in pixels (320 by default). Before the width is measured, for example while the page loads, the chart is drawn 640px wide and scaled to fit.
sections.title: Size

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the data and the text. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or text attributes.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:chart:toggle`** (cancelable) fires when a legend button is selected, with `detail.index`, `detail.hidden` and `detail.hiddenSeries`. Call `preventDefault()` to keep the series as it is.
- **`ok:chart:active`** fires with `detail.active`: the category (`{ kind: "index", index }`) or point (`{ kind: "mark", mark }`) under the pointer or the keyboard, or `null`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "chart")` returns `{ hiddenSeries, setHiddenSeries(list), active, setActive(active), setFormatters(formatters), refresh(), updateSeries(series, categories), appendData(data, options) }`. The methods don't fire events. The chart redraws by itself when the table or an option changes. See "Update data live".
- **`ok:chart:select`** fires for each value a click, Enter or Space selects or clears, with `detail.seriesIndex`, `detail.dataPointIndex`, `detail.selected` and `detail.selectedDataPoints`. See "Select data points".
- **`ok:chart:zoom`** fires when the zoom changes, with `detail.range` (`{ min, max }` or `null`) and `detail.reason`: `user` for the chart's own gestures, keys and buttons (cancelable), `group` or `brush` when a linked chart zoomed it.
- **Phase 4 methods:** `zoomRange`, `setZoomRange(range)` (its group and brushes follow), `exportChart("svg" | "png" | "csv")` (a promise that rejects outside a user gesture) and `setLocaleText(text)`.
- **Selection methods:** `selectedDataPoints`, `setSelectedDataPoints(list)` and `toggleDataPointSelection(seriesIndex, dataPointIndex)`.
- **React:** `onDataPointSelection(detail)`, controlled with `selectedDataPoints`; `onHiddenSeriesChange(hidden)` and `onActiveChange(active)`; controlled with `hiddenSeries`, uncontrolled with `defaultHiddenSeries`. The zoom: `zoomRange` / `defaultZoomRange` and `onZoomRangeChange(range, reason)`. To export from your own button, call `exportChart(figure, format)` from `@owlky/core` with the chart's `ref`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The plot is one tab stop. When it gets focus from the keyboard, the tooltip shows the first category. The arrow keys move through the categories, through the slices or rings of circular charts, or through the points of a scatter chart. Hidden slices are skipped. In heatmaps and treemaps, each arrow key moves to the nearest cell in its direction.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Give every chart a `label` (React) or a table `caption` (HTML). It names the plot and the data table.
- The data table holds every value, including hidden series. Screen readers can read it instead of the drawing, which they skip.
- The tooltip is a status region, so screen readers announce the values the keyboard moves to, and whether they are selected.
- Selected values get an outline, not only a color change, and Enter or Space selects them without a pointer.
- Marker shapes, patterns and dashes (`colorBlindMode` turns them all on) tell series apart without color, and the legend and the tooltip repeat them.
- Legend buttons report their state with `aria-pressed`. A hidden series keeps a hollow marker and crossed-out text, so the state doesn't rely on color.
- Axis labels use the secondary text color, which meets a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 in light and dark mode.
sections.title: Accessibility

sections.body:
A checkbox lets people choose any number of options from a list, or accept a single statement such as terms of use. It is a native `<input type="checkbox">`, so forms submit it, and the keyboard and assistive technology work as usual.

Put each checkbox in a **form control label**, so the text names it and clicking the text toggles it. For a setting that applies at once, use a **Switch** instead.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: In React, use `checked` with `onChange(checked)` to control the checkbox, or `defaultChecked` to let it keep its own state. `onChange` receives the new checked state. The `ref` and every other prop, such as `name`, `value` or `aria-label`, go to the input, so form libraries can register it. In HTML, read `input.checked` and listen for the native `change` event.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const input = document.querySelector("[name='newsletter']");
  // Save the setting whenever the user changes it
  input.addEventListener("change", () => saveSetting("newsletter", input.checked));
</script>
sections.title: Read and set the checked state

sections.body: The color shows when the box is checked or mixed. The default is `primary`. Use `default` for the text color, or another palette color to match the context. The `small` size has a 36px target and a 20px box, for dense layouts such as tables. The default `medium` size has a 40px target and a 24px box.
sections.title: Choose a color and size

sections.body: By default, the text follows the box (`end`). Set `labelPlacement` to `start`, `top` or `bottom` to move it. The label's negative margin lines the box up with the content edge.
sections.title: Place the label

sections.body: Pass `icon` and `checkedIcon` (and `indeterminateIcon`) to replace the box. In HTML, put your SVG inside the matching `data-ok-checkbox-icon` span. Icons follow the text color, so they take the checkbox's colors. Keep them decorative with `aria-hidden`: the label names the checkbox.
sections.title: Use your own icons

sections.body:
A parent checkbox shows a dash (mixed) when only some of its children are checked. In React, compute the state with `selectAllState` from `@owlky/core` and pass `checked` and `indeterminate`. In HTML, list the children's ids in the parent's `aria-controls`: the script checks or clears all of them, and keeps the parent's state in step.

Set `data-ok-indeterminate` (or `indeterminate` in React) for a mixed state of your own. A click by the user clears it, as with native checkboxes.
sections.title: Select all with a parent checkbox

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default. The form control label has its own options.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and behavior. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **HTML:** the input fires the native `change` event when the user toggles it. A parent's `change` updates its children without firing their `change` events. There are no instance methods.
- **React:** `onChange(checked)` is called with the new state.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The checkbox is a native input, so the browser provides the keyboard behavior.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Every checkbox needs a name: a form control label, or `aria-label` / `aria-labelledby` on the input.
- The mixed state sets the input's `indeterminate`, so screen readers announce "mixed". A parent lists its children in `aria-controls`.
- Focus is shown with a 2px ring inside the target. The target is at least 36 × 36px.
- The unchecked box uses the secondary text color, with a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Brand colors of checked boxes follow the design, so light colors such as `warning` are below 3:1 on white.
- Group related checkboxes under a heading or a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`.

sections.body: A chip is a compact element for an attribute, a filter, a choice or a small action, such as a tag on a post or an active filter. A chip can show an avatar or an icon, be clickable, and have a delete button.
sections.html: Design
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: A clickable chip is a button: pass `onClick` in React, or use a `<button data-ok-chip-action>` in HTML. Pass `onDelete` to add a delete button; Backspace or Delete on the focused chip deletes it too. In HTML, the delete button fires a cancelable `ok:chip:delete` event, then the script hides the chip. In React, remove the chip from your state in `onDelete`.
sections.title: Make a chip clickable or deletable

sections.body: Pass `href` to make the chip a link: its action becomes an `<a>` that looks and responds like a clickable chip. A link that opens a new tab with `target="_blank"` always gets `rel="noopener noreferrer"`. For a router link, pass the router's component as `component` and its own props, such as `to`, in `actionProps`. A disabled link chip has no `href`, so it can't be followed, and is marked `aria-disabled="true"`.
sections.html: Documentation Archive
sections.title: Link a chip to a page

sections.body: The variant is `filled` (default), `outlined` or `soft`. Colors are `default` (neutral), the palette colors, `black` and `white`. The `small` size is 24px high, for dense lists such as table cells.
sections.html: M Mia
sections.title: Choose a variant, color and size

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content and behavior. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:chip:delete`** (cancelable) fires when the delete button is pressed, or Backspace / Delete is pressed on the chip's button or link. If you don't call `preventDefault()`, the chip is then hidden.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "chip")` returns `{ delete() }`.
- **React:** `onDelete()` and `onClick(event)`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Clickable chips and delete buttons are native buttons.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The label names a clickable chip. Name each delete button with what it removes, such as "Remove Paris" (React: `deleteLabel`, default "Remove").
- The chip's button and its delete button are two tab stops, so keyboard users can reach both.
- A link chip is announced as a link. Use it to go somewhere, and a clickable chip to do something on the page.
- Focus is shown with a 2px outline. The delete button's target is 24 × 24px.
- Neutral chips meet a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1, and soft chips use the accessible text tone. Filled and outlined brand colors follow the design.

sections.body:
A circular progress indicator shows that something is happening. Use the **indeterminate** variant while you can't tell how long a task takes, such as loading data. Use the **determinate** variant when you know how far the task has got, such as an upload.

Each indicator is a `progressbar` for assistive technology. Give it a name that says what is loading.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Set `variant` to `determinate` and pass `value`, from `min` (default 0) to `max` (default 100). In HTML, the value is the `aria-valuenow` attribute: change it, and the runtime redraws the arc. Values outside the range are clamped.
sections.title: Show how far a task has got

sections.body: The default color is `primary`. Use another palette color, such as `success` or `error`, to match the context. Use `inherit` to take the text color of the surrounding element, for example inside a button.
sections.title: Choose a color

sections.body: The default size is 40px. Set `size` to a number of pixels, or to a CSS length in `px`, `rem` or `em` so the indicator scales with the text. `thickness` sets the stroke width, as a fraction of 44 units of the size (default 3.6). Set `enableTrackSlot` to draw a faint full circle behind the arc.
sections.title: Change the size and thickness

sections.body: Put the value next to the indicator when people need the exact number. Keep the text outside the indicator, and point `aria-labelledby` or `aria-describedby` at it if it names the task.
sections.html: 45%
sections.title: Show the value as text

sections.body: If a task usually finishes in less than a second, wait about a second before showing the indicator. Fast tasks then don't flash a spinner. Under heavy load on the main thread, the shrinking arc can stutter: set `disableShrink` to keep a fixed arc that only spins.
sections.title: Avoid flashing for fast tasks

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed or aren't valid numbers fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props name the indicator. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **HTML:** there are no events or instance methods. Change `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin`, `aria-valuemax`, `data-ok-size` or `data-ok-thickness`, and the runtime redraws the indicator. It writes private CSS custom properties through the CSS object model, so it works under a strict Content Security Policy.
- **React:** render with a new `value`. The size and the arc are set with the `style` prop. On server-rendered pages with a Content Security Policy that blocks inline styles, the determinate arc and custom sizes appear once the page hydrates.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Progress indicators don't take focus and have no keyboard interaction.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Each indicator has `role="progressbar"`. Name it with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`.
- Determinate indicators report their value with `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin` and `aria-valuemax`. For values that aren't percentages, such as "Step 3 of 5", add `aria-valuetext`.
- When an indicator stands for a region that is loading, set `aria-busy="true"` on that region until it's ready, and point the region's `aria-describedby` at the indicator.
- With reduced motion turned on, the arc stops shrinking and spins slowly, so activity stays visible.
- Brand colors follow the design. Light colors such as `warning` have a contrast ratio below 3:1 on white, so don't rely on the indicator alone to tell people something important.

sections.body:
The code editor lets people write and read source code with syntax highlighting, completion, error markers, find and replace, and a diff view. It is built on Monaco, the editor of Visual Studio Code, so both versions share the same engine and markup. A frame holds the editor, a loading message and a text area with the value.

Monaco is large, so the code editor is a separate script and Monaco itself loads only when an editor appears. Load `owlky-code-editor.js` after `owlky.js`: it loads Monaco from the `monaco/` folder next to it. With a bundler, import `@owlky/html/code-editor` or use the React components, and Monaco becomes a separate chunk of your app.
sections.html: Loading
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
In React, use `defaultValue` for the first value, or `value` and `onChange` to control it. A new `value` replaces the content as one step that people can undo, and it doesn't call `onChange`. The editor keeps what people type even when you ignore `onChange`, because Monaco can't hold back keystrokes.

In HTML, the text area holds the value. It is the editor while JavaScript loads or when Monaco can't load, and its value follows the editor, so a `name` on it sends the code with a form. Listen to `ok:code-editor:change` and call `setValue()` on the instance to replace the value.
sections.html: Loading
sections.title: Read and set the value

sections.body:
Each `path` is its own model: a file with its text, language, undo history and cursor. Change `path` to switch files. The editor creates a model the first time it sees a path, from `defaultValue` and `defaultLanguage`, and keeps it when you switch back. Turn off `saveViewState` to forget the cursor and scroll position of each file, and turn on `keepCurrentModel` to keep the model when the editor goes away.

In HTML, put each file's first text in a `<template data-ok-code-editor-model>` with its `data-ok-path` and `data-ok-language`, then change `data-ok-path` on the editor.
sections.html: Loading
sections.title: Edit several files

sections.body: The diff editor shows an original and a modified text side by side, with the changes highlighted. People can edit the modified side. Set `original` and `modified`, a `language` for both or `originalLanguage` and `modifiedLanguage`, and model paths when the texts are files. Set the option `renderSideBySide` to `false` for one column, for example on narrow screens.
sections.html: Loading
sections.title: Compare two versions

sections.body: JSON, CSS, HTML, JavaScript and TypeScript are checked as people type, and the editor underlines the problems. `onValidate` receives the current model's markers after every check, for example to list them or to block saving. In HTML, listen to `ok:code-editor:validate`. Other languages get markers only when you add them with `monaco.editor.setModelMarkers()`.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const editor = document.querySelector("[data-ok-code-editor]");
  editor.addEventListener("ok:code-editor:validate", (event) => {
    for (const marker of event.detail.markers) {
      console.log(marker.startLineNumber, marker.message);
    }
  });
</script>
sections.title: Show problems

sections.body:
Everything Monaco offers stays available. `beforeMount` receives the Monaco API before the editor exists, which is the place to register languages, completion providers and themes. `onMount` receives the editor itself, and `useMonaco()` returns the Monaco API anywhere in React once it has loaded. Pass Monaco's editor settings in `options`, such as `minimap`, `wordWrap` or `readOnly`; in HTML, write them as JSON in `data-ok-options`.

In HTML, listen to `ok:code-editor:beforemount` and `ok:code-editor:mount`, or register the editor yourself with `createCodeEditor({ beforeMount, onMount })`.
sections.html: Loading
sections.title: Use Monaco directly

sections.body:
With the default `theme` of `auto`, the editor uses Owlky's light or dark theme, whichever its scope uses through `data-ok-theme`. The colors come from your tokens and presets: the paper background, the text colors, and syntax colors that keep a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. The editor follows when the theme or preset changes.

Monaco shows one theme on a page at a time. When editors sit in scopes with different themes, the editor that people used last decides. Set `theme` to a Monaco theme such as `vs-dark` or `hc-black`, or to a theme you define in `beforeMount`, to use it instead.
sections.html:
Loading
Loading
sections.title: Match the theme

sections.body:
Owlky never loads Monaco from another site. `owlky-code-editor.js` loads it from the `monaco/` folder next to itself. To serve that folder somewhere else, copy `@owlky/html/dist/monaco/` to your server and set `data-ok-monaco-path` on the script. The folder must be on the same origin as the page, because browsers run web workers only from there.

With a bundler, Monaco is imported from the `monaco-editor` package. If your bundler doesn't find Monaco's workers by itself, pass them to `loader.config({ getWorker })`. `loader.config()` also takes `paths.vs` for your own copy of the `monaco/` folder, a `monaco` instance you already imported, and the UI language. Call it before the first editor appears.

Until Monaco is ready, the frame shows `loading` (default "Loading..."). If Monaco can't load, the text area comes back so that people can still edit the value, and `onError` or `ok:code-editor:error` reports the reason.
sections.html:
<!-- Your own copy of the monaco/ folder, in German -->
<script src="/assets/owlky-code-editor.js" data-ok-monaco-path="/assets/monaco/" defer></script>

<script type="module">
  // With a bundler: import "@owlky/html/code-editor" instead
  import { loader } from "@owlky/html/code-editor";

  loader.config({ paths: { vs: "/assets/monaco/" }, "vs/nls": { availableLanguages: { "*": "de" } } });
</script>
sections.title: Host Monaco and set up loading

sections.body:
Owlky's own code sets styles only through the CSS object model and creates no HTML from strings. Monaco needs more than the rest of Owlky, so pages with a content security policy allow it for code editor pages:

- **Styles:** `style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'`, because Monaco writes its theme and decorations into `<style>` elements.
- **Fonts and images:** `font-src 'self' data:` and `img-src 'self' data:`, because Monaco's style sheet embeds its icon font.
- **Workers:** `worker-src 'self'`.
- **Trusted Types:** the policies `owlky-code-editor`, `defaultWorkerFactory`, `diffEditorWidget`, `diffReview`, `domLineBreaksComputer`, `editorGhostText`, `editorViewLayer`, `richScreenReaderContent`, `standaloneColorizer`, `stickyScrollViewLayer`, `tokenizeToString` and `dompurify`, with `'allow-duplicates'`. The `owlky-code-editor` policy accepts only worker files from the `monaco/` folder.
sections.html: <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy" content="default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; font-src 'self' data:; img-src 'self' data:; worker-src 'self'; require-trusted-types-for 'script'; trusted-types owlky-code-editor defaultWorkerFactory diffEditorWidget diffReview domLineBreaksComputer editorGhostText editorViewLayer richScreenReaderContent standaloneColorizer stickyScrollViewLayer tokenizeToString dompurify 'allow-duplicates'">
sections.title: Set up a content security policy

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. The first table is the code editor, the second the diff editor.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the content, the loading message and Monaco itself. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or passes them in JavaScript.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:code-editor:change`** fires after every edit, with `detail.value` and Monaco's `detail.event` (`null` when people type in the text area because Monaco couldn't load).
- **`ok:code-editor:validate`** fires when the current model's markers change, with `detail.markers`.
- **`ok:code-editor:beforemount`** and **`ok:code-editor:mount`** fire with `detail.monaco` (and `detail.editor`) before and after Monaco creates the editor. The diff editor fires `ok:diff-editor:beforemount` and `ok:diff-editor:mount`.
- **`ok:code-editor:error`** and **`ok:diff-editor:error`** fire when Monaco can't load, with `detail.error`.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "code-editor")` returns `{ status, value, setValue(value), updateOptions(options), focus(), editor, monaco }`. The diff editor's instance has `original`, `modified`, `setOriginal()`, `setModified()` and `updateOptions()`.
- **React:** `onChange(value, event)`, `onValidate(markers)`, `beforeMount(monaco)`, `onMount(editor, monaco)` and `onError(error)`.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: The editor uses the keyboard shortcuts of Visual Studio Code. Tab indents the code, so it doesn't leave the editor until you switch Tab to move focus. On macOS, use Command instead of Ctrl where the table says Ctrl.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- Name the editor with `aria-label` in React (default "Code editor"), or with an `aria-label` on the text area in HTML. Monaco uses that name for its text box.
- Tab inserts a tab character. Press **Ctrl+M** (macOS: **Ctrl+Shift+M**) to make Tab and Shift+Tab move focus out of the editor, and again to switch back. Tell people about it near the editor, or set the option `tabFocusMode`.
- Press **Alt+F1** (macOS: **Option+F1**) for Monaco's accessibility help. Screen readers are detected automatically; set the option `accessibilitySupport` to `"on"` to turn the screen reader mode on yourself.
- The loading message is a status that screen readers announce, and the text area keeps the value editable when Monaco can't load.
- Syntax colors keep a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 with the editor background in Owlky's themes.

- **React props:** the props of the React component, with their types and defaults. Props that aren't listed go to the native element.
- **HTML attributes:** the options, written as `data-ok-*` attributes, with their values and defaults.

sections.title: API reference

sections.body: A collapse shows or hides its content by animating its height from 0 to the height of the content. Use it for content that opens in place, such as a nested list, the details of a row or an advanced section of a form. The element carries `hidden` while it is closed, so the content is hidden even before JavaScript runs. In the example, the switch opens four collapses: two animate their height and two their width, with and without a collapsed size.
sections.html: Shipping takes two to four working days.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
A collapse is open while it has no `hidden` attribute. Change that state, and the collapse animates to it.

- **HTML:** give a checkbox or a switch `data-ok-collapse-toggle` with the collapse's `id`: the collapse is open while the box is checked. On a button, the attribute toggles the collapse and keeps `aria-expanded` on the button up to date. One trigger can name several collapses, separated by spaces. You can also call `show()`, `hide()` or `toggle()` on the instance, or set `hidden` yourself.
- **React:** set `in` from your state. Give the button that opens it `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` with the collapse's `id`.
sections.html: Proxy, cache and logging settings.
sections.title: Open and close a collapse

sections.body: Set `orientation` to `horizontal` to animate the width instead of the height. Its children sit in a row and keep their width while it animates. Set `collapsedSize` to keep part of the content visible while the collapse is closed, such as the first 40px of a long text. It takes a number in pixels or a CSS length, such as `2.5rem`. Content in the visible part stays reachable, so don't hide controls there.
sections.html:
The first lines of the article stay visible while the collapse is closed.

Filters
sections.title: Collapse horizontally or to a size

sections.body: By default, a collapse animates over 300 ms (`--ok-duration-standard`) with the standard easing (`--ok-easing-standard`). Set `timeout` to a number of milliseconds, or to `auto` to derive the duration from the distance: about 300 ms for 120px and longer for tall content. Set `easing` to any CSS easing, such as `var(--ok-easing-decelerate)`. In React, `timeout` and `easing` also take `{ enter, exit }`; in HTML, add `data-ok-timeout-exit` and `data-ok-easing-exit`. When people turn on reduced motion in their system settings, a collapse opens and closes at once. Set `disablePrefersReducedMotion` only for an animation that carries meaning.
sections.html: Answers open with a duration that follows their height.
sections.title: Set the duration and the easing

sections.body: A collapse can be another element instead of a `div`, so it adds no wrapper. In React, pass the element or the component in `component`, along with that component's props. In HTML, add `data-ok-collapse` to the element itself. Lists use it for nested lists, tree views for the groups of child items, and vertical steppers for the content of each step. Put padding and borders on a child of the collapse, not on the collapse itself: they stay visible while it is closed. In React, `mountOnEnter` renders the children only once the collapse first opens, and `unmountOnExit` removes them once it has closed.

sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:collapse:enter`**, **`ok:collapse:entering`** and **`ok:collapse:entered`** fire on the collapse as it opens: before the animation, when it starts and when it ends.
- **`ok:collapse:exit`**, **`ok:collapse:exiting`** and **`ok:collapse:exited`** fire the same way as it closes. `detail.in` tells whether it is open.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "collapse")` returns `{ in, status, show(), hide(), toggle(force?) }`. `status` is `entering`, `entered`, `exiting` or `exited`.
- **React:** `onEnter`, `onEntering`, `onEntered`, `onExit`, `onExiting` and `onExited` get the element.

sections.body: A collapse has no keyboard interaction. The button or switch that opens it handles the keys: Enter and Space on a button, Space on a switch.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- A closed collapse carries `hidden`, so screen readers skip its content and Tab doesn't reach it. A collapsed size is the exception: the visible part stays reachable.
- Give the button that opens a collapse `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` with the collapse's `id`. The HTML trigger keeps `aria-expanded` up to date on buttons.
- The animation honors the reduced motion setting: the collapse opens and closes at once.
- When content opens below the button, focus stays on the button. Move focus into the content only when people asked for it, such as after a search.

sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
Each column has a `field` and a `headerName`. Its `type` (`string`, `number`, `date`, `dateTime`, `boolean`, `singleSelect` or `actions`) decides how it sorts, which filter operators it offers and its alignment: numbers align right.
- **Width:** `width` in pixels (100 by default), or `flex` to share the free width, with `minWidth` as a floor.
- **Values:** `valueGetter` computes a value from the row, and `valueFormatter` turns it into the text that the cell shows, the search finds and the export writes.
- **Custom cells:** `renderCell` draws anything, such as an avatar or a rating. In HTML, write that markup in the cell, and put the raw value in `data-ok-value` so sorting and filtering use it.

sections.body: **Add filter** in the filter panel adds another condition. From the second row, choose **And** (every condition must match, the default) or **Or** (any one is enough). The remove button deletes a condition. Set `disableMultipleColumnsFiltering` to keep a single condition.

sections.body:
- **Resize:** drag the end edge of a header, or press Alt + Left or Alt + Right on a focused header. A column never gets narrower than its `minWidth`. Set `resizable: false` on a column, or `disableColumnResize` on the grid, to turn it off.
- **Move:** drag a header onto another one, or choose **Move left** or **Move right** in the column menu. `columnOrder` and `onColumnOrderChange` control the order.
- **Pin:** choose **Pin to left** or **Pin to right** in the column menu. Pinned columns stay in view while the others scroll. Use `pinnedColumns` to pin columns from the start.

sections.body: Set `editable` on a column to let people change its cells: double-click a cell, or press Enter or F2. The field matches the column type: text, a number, a date, a list for `singleSelect` or a checkbox for `boolean`. Enter saves, Escape cancels, and leaving the cell saves. With `editMode="row"`, every editable cell of the row opens together. In React, `processRowUpdate` receives the new row: return it, or return a changed row. Throw or reject to refuse it. In HTML, listen to `ok:data-grid:edit` and call `preventDefault()` to refuse.
sections.html:
<script>
  // Refuse ages above 120
  grid.addEventListener("ok:data-grid:edit", (event) => {
    if (event.detail.row.age > 120) event.preventDefault();
  });
</script>
sections.title: Edit cells and rows

sections.body: The grid renders only the rows that are in view, plus a few above and below, so thousands of rows scroll smoothly. This works when the grid has a fixed height, such as `height: 520px` on the root: a grid that grows with its rows shows all of them. Set `disableVirtualization` to render every row of the page, for example before printing the page with the browser. To load more rows as people scroll, listen for the end of the rows. It's reported once for each number of rows, within `scrollEndThreshold` pixels (80 by default). Show `loading` while the next rows arrive.

sections.body: A data source lets the server sort, filter and page the rows. The grid calls `getRows()` with the sort model, the filter model and the page, and shows the rows it returns. `rowCount` is the total number of rows on the server, for the pagination. Responses are kept in a cache, so going back to a page doesn't ask the server again. Pass `dataSourceCache={null}` to turn the cache off. Errors go to `onDataSourceError` in React and to `ok:data-grid:datasourceerror` in HTML. To handle the requests yourself, set `sortingMode`, `filterMode` and `paginationMode` to `"server"`, pass `rowCount`, and load the rows in the change callbacks. While data loads, `loadingVariant` picks a progress bar, a spinner or placeholder rows (`"skeleton"`).
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const element = document.getElementById("customers");
  const grid = window.Owlky.get(element, "data-grid");
  grid.setDataSource({
    // params: { sortModel, filterModel, paginationModel: { page, pageSize } }
    async getRows(params: object) {
      const response = await fetch("/api/customers", {
        method: "POST",
        body: JSON.stringify(params),
      });
      return response.json(); // { rows, rowCount }
    },
  });
</script>
sections.title: Load rows from a server

sections.body: With a data source, the server computes the aggregated values. When the grid aggregates, `getRows()` receives `aggregationModel` (field to function), and the response adds `aggregateRow`: the values of every row that passes the filters, for the footer row. For the rows of server-side grouping and tree data, `getAggregatedValue(row, field)` reads a parent row's value, and it also reads `aggregateRow`. By default the grid reads `row[field]`. A new aggregation asks the server again. In HTML, put the model in `data-ok-aggregation-model` and give the same data source to `setDataSource()`.

sections.body: In HTML, the grid can build its rows from data instead of markup. Put one row inside `<template data-ok-data-grid-row>` in the grid: `setRows(rows)` copies it for each item, sets `data-ok-row-id` from `id`, and fills each cell with the value of its field as text. For cells with more than text, add `<template data-ok-data-grid-cell="<field>">`: its elements marked `data-ok-data-grid-value` receive the value. Values are always set as text, never as markup, so data from a server can't add scripts to the page.

sections.body: With `checkboxSelection`, people select rows with checkboxes, a click on the row, Space and Ctrl + A. Set `disableMultipleRowSelection` to allow one row at a time: selecting a row clears the others, and the header has no **Select all** checkbox. sections.body: A cell can cover the next columns with `colSpan` on its column: a number, or a function of the cell, such as a total that spans three columns. With `rowSpanning`, neighbouring cells of a column with the same text merge into one tall cell. Rows are 52 pixels tall by default. Change it with `rowHeight`; the density still scales it. In React, `getRowHeight` sets the height of each row: a number, or `"auto"` to let long text wrap and the row grow. `getRowSpacing` adds space above and below rows. In HTML, put `data-ok-row-height` and `data-ok-spacing-top` / `data-ok-spacing-bottom` on the rows. Columns can fit their content: double-click the edge of a header, set `autosizeOnMount`, or call `autosizeColumns()`.

sections.body: React has `onRowClick`, `onRowDoubleClick`, `onCellClick`, `onCellDoubleClick`, `onCellKeyDown` and `onColumnHeaderClick`. In HTML, the same events fire on the grid as `ok:data-grid:rowclick`, `ok:data-grid:cellclick` and so on. The grid's methods are the same in both versions: pass a ref from `useGridApiRef()` as `apiRef` in React, or call `runtime.get(element, "data-grid")` in HTML. For example, `exportState()` returns the sort, filters, page, columns and density, and `restoreState()` applies them again. `restoreState()` checks what it receives, so a state from storage or a URL can't change anything else.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const element = document.getElementById("people");
  const grid = window.Owlky.get(element, "data-grid");
  // Save the state as people change it, and restore it on the next visit
  grid.restoreState(JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("people-grid") ?? "{}"));
  element.addEventListener("ok:data-grid:sort", () =>
    queueMicrotask(() => localStorage.setItem("people-grid", JSON.stringify(grid.exportState()))),
  );
</script>
sections.title: React to clicks and use the grid's methods

sections.body: Check a value while people type it, and keep the cell open until it's valid. In React, return `{ error }` from the column's `preProcessEditCellProps`: `true` marks the field as invalid, and a text also shows as a message under the cell. In HTML, listen to `ok:data-grid:validate` and set `event.detail.error`. Enter and leaving the cell keep it open while the value has an error. Escape cancels. `isCellEditable` in React, or `data-ok-editable="false"` on a cell in HTML, makes single cells read-only. Typing a character on an editable cell starts editing with that character.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const element = document.getElementById("products");
  element.addEventListener("ok:data-grid:validate", (event) => {
    const { field, value } = event.detail;
    if (field === "price" && !(Number(value) > 0)) event.detail.error = "Enter a price above 0";
  });
</script>
sections.title: Check edited values

sections.body: The **is any of** operator keeps rows whose value is one of several values: type them separated by commas. A column's `filterOperators` replaces the operators of its type, for example with a range. Each operator returns a test for a value. In HTML, set them with `setFilterOperators(field, operators)`. Set `ignoreDiacritics` so that searches and filters ignore accents: "ha noi" finds "Hà Nội". `quickFilterLogicOperator="or"` keeps rows that match any word instead of every word. `quickFilterExcludeHiddenColumns` leaves hidden columns out of the search. To leave one column out, set its `getApplyQuickFilterFn` to `null` in React, or `data-ok-searchable="false"` on its header in HTML.

sections.body: **Download as CSV** exports the filtered, sorted rows of every page and the shown columns. `csvOptions` changes the delimiter, the columns (`fields`, `allColumns`), the header line and the file name. **Print** prints every filtered row on its own page, without the toolbar, footer and checkboxes. `printOptions` keeps them or picks the columns. In HTML, pass the same options to `exportCsv(options)` and `print(options)`. Values in an HTML column can be formatted with `data-ok-format` on its header (`number`, `currency`, `percent`, `date` or `datetime`) and `Intl` options in `data-ok-format-options`, or with `setValueFormatter(field, format)`.

sections.body: Locale packs translate every label: `enUS`, `viVN`, `frFR`, `deDE`, `esES`, `jaJP` and `zhCN`. Import the one you need. Pass it as `localeText` in React. In HTML, write the toolbar and menus in your language, and call `setLocaleText(pack)` for the text the grid writes itself, such as filter operators, empty states and the page range. With `dir="rtl"` on the page or a parent, the grid lays out right to left: columns pinned to the left stay at the start, which is the right side. The arrow keys follow the reading order. Set `toolbarVariant="icon"` to show the toolbar as icon buttons with tooltips.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  import { viVN } from "@owlky/core";
  window.Owlky.get(document.getElementById("people"), "data-grid").setLocaleText(viVN);
</script>
sections.title: Translate the grid and lay it out right to left

sections.body: Set `treeData` and return each row's path from `getTreeDataPath`: the names of its ancestors, then its own. Parents that a path names without a row of their own get a generated row. A group column shows the names with a button that opens and closes the children. Right and Left open and close a row when its group cell has the focus. `defaultGroupingExpansionDepth` sets how many levels are open at first. Filters keep the parents of the rows that match, and sorting orders rows among their siblings. In HTML, rows carry `aria-level` and `data-ok-parent`, and the grid fires `ok:data-grid:expand`. With a data source, `getChildrenCount` and `getGroupKey` let the grid load children when a row opens.
sections.html: Design team
sections.title: Show rows as a tree

sections.body: `getDetailPanelContent` returns what shows under a row when people open it, or `null` for rows without details. A button in the first column opens and closes the panel. `getDetailPanelHeight` sets a height in pixels; by default the content decides. In HTML, put each row's content in a `<template data-ok-data-grid-detail="<row id>">` inside the grid. The grid copies it when the panel opens and fires `ok:data-grid:detailpanel`.
sections.title: Show details under a row

sections.body: With `rowReordering`, each row gets a handle: drag it onto another row, or press Alt + Up or Alt + Down on it. A screen reader hears the new position. Moving is off while the rows are sorted or filtered. React reports moves with `onRowOrderChange`; HTML fires `ok:data-grid:roworder`, which you can cancel. `pinnedRows` keeps rows above or below the others while they scroll. Pinned rows aren't sorted, filtered or paged. In HTML, put them in `<div role="rowgroup" data-ok-data-grid-pinned-rows="top">` (or `bottom`).
sections.title: Move and pin rows

sections.body: `columnGroupingModel` puts headers over groups of columns, on as many levels as you need. A group's `description` shows as its tooltip. When a column is hidden or moved, its group splits around it. Columns can't move out of their group. `listView` shows each row as one cell, such as a card on a small screen. `listViewColumn` says which field it shows, and `renderCell` builds its content. The headers and the other cells are hidden in list view.
sections.title: Group column headers and show a list

sections.body: With `lazyLoading` and a data source, the grid asks for the rows that come into view, 50 at a time. Rows that haven't arrived show as placeholders. The data source answers `start` and `end`, and returns the total in `rowCount`. `lazyLoadingRequestThrottleMs` spaces the requests. Wide grids also render only the columns in view, when the columns have fixed widths. `rowBufferPx` and `columnBufferPx` set how much renders beyond the visible area. A data source's `updateRow` saves edited rows. Its answer is shown, and a failure brings the old values back. The cache keeps answers for five minutes, or for the `ttl` you pass to `createGridDataSourceCache`.

In tree data, the grid adds a row for each parent that a path names without a row of its own.

sections.body: A pivot summarizes the rows in a new table. `pivotModel` names the fields whose values become rows (`rows`), the fields whose values become columns (`columns`) and the fields to aggregate with their function (`values`). sections.body: With `cellSelection`, people select cells in ranges: press a cell and drag, press another cell with Shift, or hold Shift and use the arrow keys. Ctrl or Cmd adds a range, or toggles one cell. Ctrl + A selects every cell of the page. Ctrl + C copies the selected cells as tab-separated text, which spreadsheets read. Each field filters its column with the column type's first operator, and shows that operator as its label: text contains, a number equals, a date is. sections.body: The **Export** menu downloads the filtered, sorted rows as an Excel workbook. Numbers, booleans and dates keep their type, with a date format. Text is written as text, never as a formula, because exported data may come from users. `excelOptions` sets the file name, the sheet name, the fields and whether to include the headers. sections.body: With `chartsIntegration`, a chart follows the grid. `chartModel` sets its `type`, its `dimension` (the field that names the categories) and its `values` (number fields drawn as series). The types are `column`, `bar`, `line`, `area`, `pie`, `donut`, `radar` and `scatter`. When the rows are grouped, the chart shows the top-level groups with the aggregated values of the rows that pass the filters. Otherwise it shows the rows of the page. A scatter chart of rows whose category is a number column places each row at that number. The **Chart** button in the toolbar opens a panel to change the type, the category, the series, the stacking, the value labels and the legend. In HTML, the chart is a Chart component inside the grid, and the grid updates it through the chart's `updateSeries()` method.
sections.title: Chart the rows

sections.body: One grid can drive several charts. `chartModels` holds one chart model per chart id, and each model's `label` names its chart. The charts show one after the other under the grid. The **Chart** list at the top of the chart panel picks the chart the panel edits, which is `activeChartId` (`onActiveChartIdChange` reports a switch). Each chart keeps its own type, series and configuration. In HTML, put the models in `data-ok-chart-models` (JSON) with one chart region per id, and the active one in `data-ok-active-chart-id`. The grid fires `ok:data-grid:chart` with the chart's `id`, and the cancelable `ok:data-grid:activechart` when the panel switches charts.

sections.body:
The chart model also holds the chart's configuration. Each setting applies only to the types that use it.

- **`stacked`:** stacks the series of a column, bar, line or area chart. It needs two series or more.
- **`itemLabel`:** `"value"` prints the values on the chart, such as the percentages on pie slices.
- **`legend`:** places the legend at the `top`, `right` or `bottom`, or hides it with `none`. A chart with one series has no legend.
- **`colors`:** palette names or shades, such as `"info"` or `"primary-dark"`, for the series in order. Pie and donut charts use them for the slices.
- **`height`, `curve`, `showMark`, `seriesAxisLabel`, `showToolbar` and `animations`:** the plot height in pixels, the line shape, point markers, the value axis title, a toolbar with downloads and animated updates.
- **`startAngle`, `endAngle` and `donutSize`:** the angles of pie and donut slices, and the size of the donut hole in percent.

When the grid is pivoted, a value field of the pivot draws one series per pivot column, named by its keys. Grouping, filtering, pivoting and editing redraw the chart, so it always shows what the grid shows.

sections.body: Ctrl + Z (Cmd + Z on macOS) undoes the last saved edit, and Ctrl + Shift + Z or Ctrl + Y redoes it, while the focus is on a cell or a header. Each edited cell or row is one step, and so is each paste, whatever the number of cells it fills. Undo and redo save the rows again through `processRowUpdate` (HTML: a cancelable `ok:data-grid:edit`), so your server sees them like any edit. If a row changed in another way since the step, for example new `rows` from your code, the step can't apply and the steps before it are dropped. A refused save does the same. `historyStackSize` sets how many steps the grid keeps (30 by default; `0` turns undo and redo off). With `showToolbar`, the toolbar has **Undo** and **Redo** buttons. In React, `showHistoryControls={false}` hides them. In HTML, they're the toolbar buttons with `data-ok-data-grid-history`. `apiRef.current.history` (HTML: the instance's `history`) has `undo()`, `redo()`, `canUndo()`, `canRedo()` and `clear()`. `onUndo` and `onRedo` (HTML: `ok:data-grid:undo` and `ok:data-grid:redo`) report the ids of the rows that changed. Typing in a field keeps the field's own undo.

sections.body: A click on a header goes through ascending, descending and not sorted. `sortingOrder` changes that cycle for every column, and a column's own `sortingOrder` for that column. For example, `["desc", "asc", null]` sorts the biggest values first, and a cycle without `null` never goes back to not sorted. The column menu only offers the directions of the cycle. A column's `sortComparator` compares two values in ascending order, and the grid reverses it for descending. `getSortComparator(direction)` returns a comparator per direction that the grid uses as it is, for example to keep empty values last in both directions. In HTML, write the cycle as JSON in `data-ok-sorting-order` on the grid or on a header, and set comparators with `setSortComparator(field, { sortComparator, getSortComparator })`. HTML comparators get the cells' values as text. With `multipleColumnsSortingMode="always"`, every click adds the column to the sort, without Shift.

sections.body: A column with `filterVariant: "set"` filters with a checklist of its values, like a spreadsheet. It works for text, number and single select columns. The list holds each value of the column once, in the column's order, with a search field and **Select all**. **Select all** checks the values the search shows, or clears them when they're all checked. The checked values make an `isAnyOf` filter item, so the filter model stays the same as with the other operators: `{ field, operator: "isAnyOf", value: ["High", "Low"] }`. Clear every value to remove the filter. With `headerFilters`, the header filter is a button that shows the choice, such as "2 selected", and opens the checklist. In the filter panel, the checklist takes the value field's place while the operator is "is any of". In HTML, write `data-ok-filter-variant="set"` on the header cell. The grid copies the first checklist of the markup, such as a header filter's, for the panel.

sections.body: With tree data or grouped rows and `checkboxSelection`, a selection reaches related rows. Selecting a parent selects its children, and selecting all children selects the parent. A parent with only some selected children shows a mixed checkbox. Each group row of grouped rows gets a checkbox that selects its rows. Group rows never enter the selection model: their checkbox shows the state of their rows. `rowSelectionPropagation` turns each direction on or off: `{ descendants: true, parents: false }` keeps parents out. Only rows that pass the filters follow. `checkboxColDef` sets the checkbox column's `width`, `headerClassName` and `cellClassName`. `rowSelection={false}` turns selection off, so no checkboxes show and clicks select nothing. In HTML, write the propagation as JSON in `data-ok-row-selection-propagation` and `data-ok-row-selection="false"` to turn selection off.

sections.body: Each column can turn grid features off for itself. `hideSortIcons` hides the sort arrow, while the header still sorts. `disableColumnMenu` removes the column's menu. `disableReorder` keeps the column in its place: it doesn't drag, and other columns can't move past it. `disableExport` leaves it out of the CSV, Excel and print exports. `pinnable: false` hides the pin items of its menu. `cellClassName` and `headerClassName` add class names, as a string or from a function, so your CSS can style a column or single cells. `rowHeader: true` makes the column's cells row headers (`role="rowheader"`), so screen readers announce them with the other cells of the row. `display: "flex"` lays out cell content in a row, centered. With `rowSpanning`, `rowSpanValueGetter` returns the value that neighbouring cells compare to merge, such as the owner within a team. `pastedValueParser` turns pasted text into the cell's value.
