sections.body:
A map shows places and data that people can pan, zoom, tilt and turn. It is drawn by MapLibre GL JS, an open-source map engine, so both versions share the same behavior and markup. Around the map, Owlky draws its own controls, markers, popups and panels, which follow your theme and work with the keyboard.

The map is a separate script so that pages without one don't download the map engine. Load `owlky-map.js` after `owlky.js`. It finds its worker, `owlky-map-worker.js`, next to itself. With npm, import `@owlky/html/map` (HTML) or use the map components of `@owlky/react`, and point `setMapWorkerUrl()` at `@owlky/core/map-worker.js`.

Owlky includes no map tiles. Pass the URL of a MapLibre style, for example one of OpenFreeMap's free styles, and keep the credits that the style requires.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
`mapStyle` sets the style: a URL of a MapLibre style JSON, or the style object itself. Add `mapStyleDark` to switch styles when the map sits in a dark theme, such as the **Theme** menu's dark mode or a `data-ok-theme="dark"` area. Without it, the map keeps one style in both themes.

In HTML, change `data-ok-map-style` to switch the style later. In React, pass a new `mapStyle`, and keep style objects in a constant or `useMemo`, because a new object reloads the style.

Layer colors can use Owlky tokens: write `"var(--ok-palette-info-main)"` as a paint value. The map reads the token's value, and reads it again when the theme changes.
sections.title: Choose the map style

sections.body:
A marker sits on a point given by `longitude` and `latitude`. By default it is a pin in the `color` you choose. Set `anchor` to `bottom` for pins, so the tip touches the point. Give interactive markers a name with `aria-label`: a marker with a click handler or `draggable` is a button that people reach with Tab.

A popup is a dialog that points at a place. It picks the side where it fits unless you set `anchor`, and `offset` moves it away from its marker. Escape, the close button and a click on the map close it. In React, a popup shows while you render it, and `onClose` asks you to remove it. In HTML, write popups with `hidden` and open them from a marker with `data-ok-map-popup-open`.

With `draggable`, people drag a marker or move it with the arrow keys. In HTML the marker stores its new position in its attributes. In React, update `longitude` and `latitude` in `onDragEnd`. Also let people place a marker with a click, because dragging is hard for some people.

A source holds data, such as GeoJSON points or polygons, and its layers draw it as circles, fills, lines, labels or a heatmap. The `paint`, `layout` and `filter` values follow the MapLibre style specification. A GeoJSON source can group nearby points in clusters with `cluster`.

In HTML, sources and layers are hidden elements inside the map. Write their `paint`, `layout` and `filter` as JSON in single-quoted attributes. Change an attribute, for example `data-ok-filter`, and the map updates the layer. For data that changes every frame, call `setSourceData(id, data)` on the instance instead.

sections.body: List the layers people can point at in `interactiveLayerIds` (HTML: `data-ok-interactive-layer-ids`, separated by spaces). Mouse events then report the features under the pointer in `features`, and the cursor turns into a pointer over them. `onMouseEnter` and `onMouseLeave` fire when the pointer enters or leaves those features. Use them for highlights and hover popups. Give a hover popup `closeButton={false}`, `closeOnClick={false}` and `focusAfterOpen={false}`.

sections.title: Respond to the pointer

sections.body:
A choropleth colors regions, such as countries or states, by a value. `mapScale(values, options)` sorts the values into classes and returns the class breaks, one color per class and a MapLibre expression that paints them. Pick the `method`: `quantile` (about as many regions in each class, the default), `equalInterval` (classes of the same width), `jenks` (natural breaks that keep similar values together) or `threshold` (your own `thresholds`). The colors come from the shades of a palette color, such as `primary`, so they follow the theme and the preset. Pass your own colors in `palette` if you need more than five classes.

`mapRegionLayers({ id, source, scale })` returns two layers: a fill in the scale's colors and an outline that marks the region under the pointer, the one the keyboard is on and the selected one. The source needs a feature id for each region, so set `promoteId` to the property that names it.

`MapRegions` joins your data to those regions by id (HTML: a `div[data-ok-map-regions]` with a table). It also gives keyboard users a list of the regions: press Tab to reach it, then use the arrow keys to move from region to region and hear its name and value. Enter selects a region, like a click on the map. The table holds the same data for screen readers, and the map shows it when the browser can't draw the map.

`MapLegend` shows the classes in a corner of the map. Each class is a toggle button: press one or more to fade the regions outside them. Set `variant` to `gradient` for a continuous bar, and draw the fill with `scale.gradient` (`mapRegionLayers` with `variant: "gradient"`).

Controls sit in the corners of the map: `NavigationControl` (zoom and a compass you can drag to turn the map), `GeolocateControl`, `FullscreenControl`, `ScaleControl`, `GlobeControl`, `TerrainControl` and `AttributionControl`, which every map shows unless you turn it off with `attributionControl={false}`. sections.body: The map accepts only `http` and `https` URLs for styles, data and tiles, and shows the credits of a style as text and links, never as HTML. Its engine draws in a Web Worker. With a Content Security Policy, allow the worker with `worker-src 'self'`, and add `blob:` when the worker comes from another origin, such as a CDN. Pages that enforce Trusted Types need a policy for the worker's URL.

sections.body: These props set the style, the content and the callbacks. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or listens to events.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:map:load`**, **`ok:map:move`**, **`ok:map:moveend`**, **`ok:map:click`**, **`ok:map:mousemove`**, **`ok:map:mouseenter`**, **`ok:map:mouseleave`** and the other map events fire on the map with `detail.viewState`, and for pointer events `lngLat`, `point` and `features`.
- **`ok:map:popupopen`** and **`ok:map:popupclose`** fire on a popup. `popupclose` has `detail.reason` and can be canceled to keep it open.
- **`ok:map:markerdragstart`**, **`ok:map:markerdrag`** and **`ok:map:markerdragend`** fire on a marker with `detail.lngLat`.
- **`ok:map:regionselect`** fires on a `div[data-ok-map-regions]` with `detail.id`, which is `null` when the selection is cleared. **`ok:map:legendtoggle`** fires on a legend with `detail.classIndex` and `detail.active`, the pressed classes.
- **`ok:map:fullscreen`**, **`ok:map:geolocate`**, **`ok:map:geolocateerror`**, **`ok:map:trackuserlocation`** and **`ok:map:fallback`** report the controls and a map that can't draw.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "map")` returns `{ map, controller, viewState, flyTo, easeTo, jumpTo, fitBounds, setSourceData(id, data), getClusterExpansionZoom(source, id), openPopup(popup), closePopup(popup), fullscreen, setFullscreen(on), scale(values, options) }`. `scale` is `mapScale`, for pages that load the map from the CDN.

sections.body:
Markdown turns Markdown text into styled content: headings, paragraphs, links, lists, task lists, tables, code, images and quotes. It reads GitHub Flavored Markdown by default. Both versions run the same parser, built on unified, and build the content with DOM methods or React elements, never from an HTML string.

Markdown is a separate script so that pages without it don't download the parser. Load `owlky-markdown.js` after `owlky.js`, or import `@owlky/html/markdown` after `@owlky/html/auto`. In HTML, write the Markdown inside a `pre[data-ok-markdown-source]` element. Escape `&` and `<` as `&` and `<`, as for any text in HTML. Without JavaScript, the page shows the Markdown text itself.

By default, HTML in the Markdown shows as text, so content from people can't add elements to your page. Turn on `rawHtml` to render it. The HTML then goes through an allow list, the same one GitHub uses, plus `u`, `mark` and the `text-align` and `text-transform` styles. Scripts, event handler attributes, forms, frames and unknown elements are removed. Turn on `skipHtml` to drop the HTML instead.

To allow more, pass your own `sanitizeSchema`. Extend `markdownSanitizeSchema` rather than writing one from scratch, because a missing rule can let unsafe markup through.

Every URL in `href`, `src` and similar attributes goes through `urlTransform`. The default, `defaultUrlTransform`, keeps relative URLs and the `http`, `https`, `mailto`, `irc`, `ircs` and `xmpp` protocols, and empties anything else, such as `javascript:` or `data:` URLs. Pass your own function to rewrite URLs, for example to send images through a proxy. Keep the default checks in it, because an unchecked URL can run script when it is clicked.

Turn on `externalLinks` to open absolute `http` and `https` links in a new tab. Links that open a new tab always get `rel="noopener noreferrer"`.

sections.body: Motion animates its content in or out. By default, it plays when the content scrolls into view, so long pages reveal their sections as you read. The animation comes from the stylesheet. The script only decides when it plays. Without the script, the content shows as usual, so nothing stays hidden. Users who ask for reduced motion see the content appear at once.
sections.html: Plans for every team
sections.title: Overview

sections.body:
`variant` names the animation. Entrances end with the content in place, and exits end with it hidden.
- **Slide, fade, zoom and bounce:** `slideInUp`, `fadeIn`, `zoomOutLeft`, `bounceInDown` and more. `Up` and `Down` name the movement, `Left` and `Right` the side it comes from or goes to.
- **Flip, scale and rotate:** `flipInX`, `flipOutY`, `scaleInX`, `scaleOutY`, `rotateIn` and `rotateOut`.
- **Backgrounds:** `kenburnsTop` and the other Ken Burns directions zoom slowly into an image. `panTop` and the other pan directions move a gradient background. `color2x` to `color5x` paint text with a moving gradient. These loop until you pause them.

`duration` sets the length of an entrance in milliseconds (640 by default), `delay` waits before it starts, and `distance` sets how far directional animations travel in pixels.
sections.html: Welcome back
sections.title: Choose an animation

sections.body:
`trigger` decides when the animation plays:
- **`inView` (default):** when at least `amount` of the content is visible (0.3 by default). It plays once. Set `once` to `false` to play the exit when the content leaves the view and the entrance again when it comes back.
- **`mount`:** as soon as the page loads, for content that is visible from the start.
- **`manual`:** when you set `in`. Turning `in` off plays the animation backwards. In HTML, add or remove the `data-ok-in` attribute.

Changing `variant`, `duration` or `distance` plays an entered animation again. In HTML, `replay()` plays it again too. In React, change the `key`.
sections.html: Saved
sections.title: Decide when it plays

sections.body:
With the `inView` trigger, two options change what counts as the view:
- **`viewportMargin`:** grows the view, or shrinks it with negative values, before the visible part is measured. Write it like CSS margins in `px` or `%`. For example, `0px 0px -100px` plays the animation once the content is 100 pixels above the bottom edge. In HTML, use the `data-ok-viewport-margin` attribute.
- **`viewportRoot`:** a scrolling container that holds the content, used as the view instead of the browser window. In React, pass a ref to it. In HTML, write its `id` in `data-ok-viewport-root`.

`onViewportEnter` runs when the content enters the view, and `onViewportLeave` when it leaves. In HTML, listen for the `ok:motion:enter` and `ok:motion:leave` events. MotionGroup and MotionText have the same options and events. With `once` on (the default), only the first entrance is reported, so set `once` to `false` to hear every one.

sections.body: Ken Burns, pan and color animations keep moving. Give your users a way to pause them, because moving content that lasts more than five seconds distracts many people. Set `paused` from your own control, such as a switch or a button.

sections.body:
Two variants aren't entrances:
- **`draw`:** traces the strokes of an SVG, then fades its fill in. Give every shape `pathLength="1"`, so the stroke length is known.
- **`interactive`:** scales the content up on hover and down while it's pressed, such as a card or a button. The element shrinks to its content. Icon buttons and floating action buttons have their own `animate` option for the same effect.

sections.body: CountUp counts from `start` (0 by default) to `end` when it scrolls into view, in 2 seconds by default. Set `decimals` for digits after the decimal point, and `prefix` or `suffix` for units. Screen readers read the end value from the start, because the changing digits are hidden from them. Digits keep the same width, so the text doesn't shake.
sections.html: 200k 0k
sections.title: Count up to a number

sections.body:
MotionBorder draws a moving border around its content, such as a logo, an avatar or a button.

- **Color:** `multi` (the default) turns several brand colors all around. `inherit` (the text color) or a palette color runs one light along a faint track of the same color.
- **Second light:** `secondaryColor` adds a light in another color that starts on the opposite side. It has no effect with `multi`.
- **Shape and size:** set `shape` to `circle` for round content, `width` for the border width in pixels and `duration` for one turn.
- **Edges and corners:** the border follows the element's CSS. Set `border-width` to `0` on a side to leave it out, and set `border-radius` per corner. Your rules win over the library's, because its selectors have zero specificity.

The inside is painted with the paper color, so put the border on a paper or a page background.
sections.title: Turn a border around content

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop in React, an attribute in HTML. Values that aren't listed fall back to the default.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup or reads them from the page.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:motion:end`** fires on a Motion when its animation ends, with the state in `detail.state`: `enter` or `exit`.
- **`ok:motion:enter` and `ok:motion:leave`** fire on a Motion with the `inView` trigger when it enters or leaves the view, with the visible fraction in `detail.ratio`. MotionGroup and MotionText fire `ok:motion-group:enter`, `ok:motion-text:enter` and the matching `leave` events. A Motion inside a group fires none: the group reports for it.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "motion")` returns `{ state, replay() }`. MotionGroup (`"motion-group"`) and MotionText (`"motion-text"`) have the same instance. `replay()` plays the entrance again.
- **React:** use `onAnimationEnd`, `onViewportEnter` and `onViewportLeave` (they receive the `IntersectionObserverEntry`), and change the `key` to play the entrance again.

sections.body: Motion isn't interactive. Links and buttons inside it work as usual, also while they move.

sections.body:
- Content never depends on the animation: without the script, it shows, and with reduced motion it appears at once.
- Looping animations and turning borders stop with reduced motion. Provide a pause control for them anyway (WCAG 2.2.2).
- CountUp exposes its end value to assistive technologies, and hides the changing digits.
- MotionText keeps the text readable: assistive technologies read a visually hidden copy, and the letters are hidden from them.
- Avoid animations on content that people need to read right away, such as errors.
- Directional animations start outside the content's box. Clip the container (`overflow: clip`) if they would widen the page on small screens.

sections.body: An organization chart shows a hierarchy as a tree, such as the people of a company or the parts of a product. Each node holds any content you choose, such as a card with a name and a role. Lines join every node to its parent. The chart is a set of nested lists (`ul` and `li`), so screen readers announce each level and how many nodes it has. It needs no JavaScript.
sections.html:
• Maya Lindqvist, CEO
    • Jonah Pereira, design
    • Priya Raman, development
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: `OrganizationChart` is the root: its `label` is the top node and its children are the next level. Each `OrganizationChartNode` has a `label` and may hold more nodes, at any depth. In HTML, a node is an `li` with a label `div` and, when it has children, a `ul` of child nodes. Leave out the children list on nodes without children, so no line hangs below them. Labels take any content, such as cards with an avatar, a name, a role and a menu button.
sections.html:
• Priya Raman
    • Elias Novak
sections.title: Build the tree

sections.body: The line options are set on the root and apply to the whole chart. `lineColor` is `divider` by default. Set it to a palette color for its light tone, or to `inherit` to use the chart's text color, which you can set with the `color` property. `lineStyle` draws `solid`, `dashed` or `dotted` lines. Lengths are numbers in pixels, or strings with a unit such as `"1.5rem"`: `lineHeight` (40 by default) is the height of the lines between two levels, `lineWidth` (1) their thickness, `lineBorderRadius` (24) the corner radius where they turn and `nodePadding` (4) the space on each side of every node. In HTML, the lengths need the script: it turns the attributes into private CSS properties, because CSS can't read lengths from attributes. Without the script, the default lengths apply.
sections.html:
• Maya Lindqvist, CEO
    • Jonah Pereira, design
    • Priya Raman, development
sections.title: Style the lines

sections.body: A chart is as wide as its widest level and is centered when it fits. Put it in a `Scrollbar` so that a wide chart scrolls sideways inside the page, from its first node, instead of widening the page on small screens. Name the scroll area: it takes keyboard focus so that keyboard users can scroll it.
sections.html:
• Maya Lindqvist, CEO
    • Jonah Pereira, design
    • Priya Raman, development
sections.title: Scroll wide charts

sections.body:
`direction` sets the side the top node sits on, and the chart grows away from it:

- **`top`:** the default. Children sit below their parent.
- **`bottom`:** children sit above their parent.
- **`left`:** the top node sits at the start of the line, and children follow toward the end. In a right-to-left page, the chart mirrors and grows toward the left.
- **`right`:** the reverse of `left`.

Horizontal charts suit deep trees with short labels: each level adds width instead of height. Every direction keeps the same markup, so screen readers, the reading order and the **Tab** order follow the tree, parent before children, whatever the layout. Toggle buttons sit on the side of the label that faces the children, and their arrow points at them. The direction doesn't change with the screen width. To use another direction on small screens, change the prop or the attribute from your own code, for example after `matchMedia("(max-width: 600px)")` matches.
sections.html:
• Maya Lindqvist, CEO
    • Jonah Pereira, design
    • Priya Raman, development
sections.title: Choose a direction

sections.body: Set `enableExpandCollapse` to give every node with children a toggle button on the bottom edge of its label. The button collapses the node's children and expands them again, with an animation. A collapsed node draws no lines below it, and its button shows how many nodes it hides. Every node starts expanded: list the ids of the nodes to collapse at first in `defaultCollapsedNodes`, or control them with `collapsedNodes` and `onCollapsedNodesChange`. Give each node a `nodeId` and a `toggleLabel`, such as "Priya Raman's reports", which names its button for screen readers. Set `expandCollapseOnNodeClick` to also toggle a node when someone clicks its label, outside its own buttons and links. In HTML, the markup holds the state: a collapsed node's children list has `hidden` and its button has `aria-expanded="false"`. The script toggles both.

• Maya Lindqvist, CEO
    • Jonah Pereira, design
    • Priya Raman, development
      • Elias Novak
      • Noah Brennan

import { OrganizationChart, OrganizationChartNode } from "@owlky/react";

export function CollapsibleCompany() {
  return (
    <OrganizationChart
      aria-label="Company"
      enableExpandCollapse
      expandCollapseOnNodeClick
      defaultCollapsedNodes={["priya"]}
      nodeId="maya"
      toggleLabel="Maya Lindqvist's reports"
      label="Maya Lindqvist, CEO"
    >
      <OrganizationChartNode nodeId="jonah" label="Jonah Pereira, design" />
      <OrganizationChartNode
        nodeId="priya"
        toggleLabel="Priya Raman's reports"
        label="Priya Raman, development"
      >
        <OrganizationChartNode nodeId="elias" label="Elias Novak" />
        <OrganizationChartNode nodeId="noah" label="Noah Brennan" />
      </OrganizationChartNode>
    </OrganizationChart>
  );

- **Highlight on hover:** with `highlightOnHover`, hovering a node or moving the focus into it highlights its path to the top node: the lines on the path take the primary color, and the other nodes fade. `dimOpacity` sets how much they fade, from 0 (not at all) to 1 (hidden), and is 0.7 by default.
- **Highlight from code:** `highlightNode(nodeId)` highlights a node and its path until `clearHighlight()`. It opens the collapsed nodes above it, then scrolls it into view, and returns a promise that resolves once it is in view. The node gets a ring and `data-ok-highlighted`, and nothing fades, so that every node keeps its text contrast while the result shows. Hovering another node highlights that node instead, for as long as the pointer stays.
- **Search:** put an `Autocomplete` next to the chart, with one option per node and the node's id as the option's value. When the value changes, call `highlightNode(value)`, and write what happened in a `role="status"` element, so that screen readers announce it politely.

In React, the highlighted node is the `highlightedNode` prop (or `defaultHighlightedNode`), reported through `onHighlightedNodeChange`. In HTML, it is the `data-ok-highlighted` attribute on the node, and the instance has `highlightNode(nodeId)`, `clearHighlight()` and `getHighlightedNode()`.

sections.body: A node can load its children the first time it expands, such as from a server. In React, set `hasChildren` on the node and pass `loadChildren` to the chart: it receives the node's id and resolves with the child nodes. In HTML, give the node a toggle and an empty, hidden children list, then answer the `ok:organization-chart:loadchildren` event with `detail.respondWith()`, which takes child node elements or a promise of them. While the children load, the toggle shows a progress indicator and has `aria-busy="true"`. When no children come back, the node becomes a leaf. When the promise is rejected, the node stays collapsed and the next expand tries again. Children load once: catch errors in your loader to show a message, and reject so that people can retry.

- Lines are decorative: the list structure carries the hierarchy. Don't rely on a line color alone to convey meaning.

- A click on a label is a shortcut for pointer users: keyboard users reach the toggle button with **Tab**.
- The hover highlight follows the keyboard focus too, so keyboard users see the same path. Faded nodes stay readable but drop below the text contrast minimum while the highlight lasts: set `dimOpacity` to 0 to keep full contrast, as the path's colors still show it.

sections.body:
A select lets people choose one or more options from a list. The field shows the current value. A press, or a key such as Arrow Down, opens a menu of options under it. It is made of these parts:

- **FormControl:** the root. It shares the variant, the size and the states with the select, its label and its helper text.
- **InputLabel:** the label. It rests inside the field and moves above it when the field has focus or a value.
- **Select:** the field. Its options are **MenuItem**s, shown in a menu on the page's top layer.
- **FormHelperText:** a hint or an error message under the field.

In HTML, the select needs the JavaScript runtime: it opens the menu, moves focus through the options and writes the value. The value also sits in a hidden input, so the select works in a `<form>`. With `native`, the field is the browser's own `<select>` and needs no JavaScript.

sections.body: A slider picks a value, or a range of two values, along a track, such as a volume or a price range. Each thumb holds a native range input: the keyboard, screen readers and forms work as they do for `<input type="range">`. People drag a thumb, or press the track to move the nearest thumb there, with a mouse, a finger or a pen.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: `min`, `max` and `step` set the values (0, 100 and 1 by default). `marks` draws a tick at every step (`true`), or at the values you list, each with an optional label below the track. Set `step` to `null` to allow only the marked values. In HTML, write one `data-ok-slider-mark` per mark and set `data-ok-step="0"` for marks only.
sections.html: 0°C 20°C 100°C
sections.title: Set steps and marks

sections.body: `valueLabelDisplay` shows the value in a bubble above the thumb: `auto` while the thumb is hovered, focused or dragged, `on` always. `valueLabelFormat` sets its text, and `getAriaValueText` what screen readers announce, such as "30°C". In HTML, `data-ok-label-value="{value}°C"` sets both.
sections.html: 30°C
sections.title: Show the value

sections.body: Pass two values to get two thumbs. Name each one with `getAriaLabel`, for example "Minimum price". A thumb that passes the other one swaps places with it, unless you set `disableSwap`. `onChange` fires while the value changes, and `onChangeCommitted` once a drag or a key press ends: use it for costly work such as a search.
sections.title: Pick a range

sections.body: `size` is `medium` (a 10px track) or `small` (6px). `color` is a palette color or `inherit`. `track` is `normal`, `inverted` (filled from the value to the end) or `false`. Set `orientation` to `vertical` for a slider that fills its container's height: give that container a height.
sections.title: Change the look

sections.body: In React, `scale` turns the value into the one people see and hear, such as a power of two for a storage size. The value label, `getAriaValueText` and `aria-valuenow` get the scaled value, while `onChange` keeps the plain one. In HTML, call `setScale(scale, format)` on the instance: `format` writes the value label and `aria-valuetext`.

<!-- The slider of the "Non-linear scale" story -->
<script type="module">
  import { getRuntime } from "@owlky/html";

  const slider = getRuntime().get(document.querySelector("[data-ok-slider]"), "slider");
  slider.setScale(
    (value) => 2 ** value,
    (bytes) => `${bytes / 1024} KB`,
  );
</script>

sections.body: A snackbar, or toast, shows a brief message at the edge of the screen and closes by itself after 4 seconds. Render one toaster per page. Then show toasts from anywhere: with the `toast()` function in React, or with a `<template>` and a button in HTML. Toasts pause while you hover over or focus the toaster.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: Use `toast.info`, `toast.success`, `toast.warning` or `toast.error` for a toast with a colored icon. `toast.promise` shows a loading toast and replaces it with the result. In HTML, set `data-ok-type` on the toast; a loading toast with `data-ok-then` is replaced by another template when its time (`data-ok-duration`) runs out, and the instance's `promise()` method follows a real promise.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const toaster = window.Owlky.get(document.querySelector("[data-ok-toaster]"), "toaster");
  toaster.show({ type: "success", title: "Event created", description: "Monday at 6:00 PM" });
  toaster.promise(fetch("/api/save"), { loading: "Saving", success: "Saved", error: "Not saved" });
</script>
sections.title: Show the status

sections.body: Pass `action: { label, onClick }` to add a button, such as **Undo**. The toast closes when it is clicked, unless the handler calls `preventDefault()`. Pass your own nodes as `action` for several buttons. Toasts with an action have no close button.
sections.title: Add an action

sections.body: Set `position` to a corner or the center of the top or bottom edge. At the bottom, the newest toast sits nearest to the edge. In HTML, a trigger with `data-ok-toaster-position` moves the toaster before it shows its toast.
sections.title: Move the toaster

sections.body: By default the toasts are listed one under another. Set `expand` to `false` to stack them: the newest toast stays in front and two more peek out behind it. The stack expands while the pointer or the focus is in it. Press **Alt + T** to expand it from the keyboard and move the focus to the toasts, and press **Escape** to collapse it again. Change the keys with `hotkey`, such as `["ctrlKey", "KeyM"]` (HTML: `data-ok-hotkey="ctrlKey+KeyM"`), or pass `[]` to turn it off.
sections.title: Stack toasts

sections.body: People can swipe a toast toward the edge of the screen to close it: up or down, and toward the side for toasts in a corner. A short swipe springs back. Set `swipeDirections` to choose the directions, or pass `[]` to turn swiping off (HTML: `data-ok-swipe-directions`, empty to turn it off). Because a swipe needs a dragging movement, every toast that can be swiped also shows a close button, unless you set `closeButton` to `false`. Keyboard users close a focused toast with **Escape**.
sections.title: Swipe toasts away

sections.body: Set `richColors` to give success, info, warning and error toasts their status color: the dark tone of the color on its light tone. Set `invert` to reverse the colors: plain toasts become light and typed toasts dark. Both work on the toaster, for every toast, or on one toast, where `false` turns the toaster's setting off. In HTML, put `data-ok-rich-colors` or `data-ok-invert` on the toaster or on a toast (`="false"` turns it off for that toast).
sections.title: Color toasts

sections.body: A toast can ask for another position than the toaster's with its own `position`: it then shows in a list of its own at that position. `offset` sets the distance from the edges of the screen (16px by default) as a number of pixels, a CSS length such as `2rem`, or one value per side. `mobileOffset` does the same on screens under 600px wide, and `gap` sets the space between toasts (12px). For right-to-left languages, set `dir="rtl"` on the toaster: the icon, the text and the close button swap sides.
sections.title: Place toasts and change the spacing

sections.body: Give a toaster an `id` to keep it apart: it shows only the toasts whose `toasterId` names it, and a toaster without an `id` shows the others. In HTML, each toaster has its own instance, and a trigger picks one with `data-ok-toast-toaster`. In React, `toastOptions` sets defaults for every toast of a toaster, such as `duration` or `closeButton`, and `icons` replaces the type icons and the close icon.
sections.title: Use several toasters and set defaults

sections.body: `toast.promise()` shows the `loading` message until the promise settles, then `success` or `error` in the same toast. It also takes toast options, such as `position` or `duration`, and `finally`, which runs after the result shows. It returns the toast's id with an `unwrap()` method that gives the promise's own result. The id is an object, so compare it with `id.valueOf()`. `toast.getToasts()` returns the toasts shown now, `toast.getHistory()` every toast shown so far, and the `useSonner()` hook keeps a component up to date with the toasts. In HTML, the instance has `promise()` with `finally`, `getToasts()` and `getHistory()`.
sections.title: Follow a promise and read the toasts

sections.body: Every option works the same way in both versions: a prop of `Toaster` in React, an attribute of the toaster in HTML.
sections.title: Options

sections.body: These are the `toast()` options. In HTML they are the toast's markup and attributes.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:toaster:show`** (`detail.toast`) and **`ok:toaster:dismiss`** (`detail.toast`, `detail.reason`: `close`, `dismiss`, `action`, `cancel`, `timeout`, `escape`, `swipe`, `api` or `overflow`) fire on the toaster.
- **`ok:toaster:action`** (cancelable) fires before an action or cancel button closes its toast.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(toaster, "toaster")` returns `{ show(options), showTemplate(template), promise(promise, messages), dismiss(id?), getToasts(), getHistory() }`. `show()` builds the toast from text, never from HTML.
- **React:** `toast()` returns the toast's id; `toast.dismiss(id?)` closes one toast or all of them. `onDismiss` and `onAutoClose` report how it closed.
sections.title: Events and methods

sections.body: Toasts don't take focus when they appear, so they never interrupt typing.
sections.title: Keyboard

sections.body:
- The toast list is a polite live region: screen readers announce new toasts without interrupting.
- Time pauses while the pointer or focus is in the toaster, so people can read and act.
- Don't rely on a toast for anything that must be done: it closes by itself. Use a Dialog instead.
- Swiping is never the only way to close a toast: swipeable toasts show a close button, and **Escape** closes a focused toast.
- Rich colors pair each status color's dark tone with its light tone, at a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.
- Icons are decorative; the title carries the message. Typed toasts keep their text at a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1.

sections.body:
A sortable list lets people put items in their own order, such as tasks by priority or widgets on a dashboard. Each item has a handle: drag it with a mouse, finger or pen, move it with the keyboard, or tap two handles to swap places. Items can also have a remove button.

Every move is announced to screen reader users, such as "Moved to position 2 of 4".
sections.html:
• Design
  • Build
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: `grid` (the default) arranges items in columns that fit the width, `vertical` stacks them in one column and `horizontal` puts them in one row. Wrap a vertical or horizontal list in a **Scrollbar**: it scrolls the list and draws its frame.
sections.html:
• Sales
  • Orders
  • Visitors
sections.title: Choose a layout

sections.body: In React, pass `onRemove`: every item gets a remove button, and you update your data. In HTML, add a `data-ok-sortable-remove` button to each item; the script removes the item. Remove buttons appear when the pointer rests on an item or focus is inside it, and are always visible on touch screens.
sections.html: • Design
sections.title: Let people remove items

sections.body: Adding is up to you. In React, add to your data. In HTML, put a `<template data-ok-sortable-template>` with the new item's markup in the list, and a button with `data-ok-sortable-add="<list id>"`. The script clones the template and fires `ok:sortable:add`, where you fill in the new item.
sections.html:
• Design
  • Build
sections.title: Add items

sections.body:
Give lists the same group to let people move items between them, such as tasks on a board. In HTML, add `data-ok-group` and an `id` to each list; the script moves the items. In React, pass `group` and `id`, and update your data in `onTransfer`. The `moveBetweenLists(lists, event)` helper updates data kept as an object of arrays by list id.

People drag an item onto another list, even an empty one. With the keyboard, they grab an item, then press the Left or Right arrow key in vertical lists, or the Up or Down arrow key in horizontal lists. In a grid, the arrow keys move past the first or last item into the previous or next list. Focus stays on the moved item, and screen readers hear the list's name, such as "Moved to Done, position 1 of 2".

To limit where items go, set `accept` (`data-ok-accept` in HTML) to the groups a list takes items from. For example, a list in the group `archive` with `accept="board"` takes items from the board but gives none back.
sections.html:
• Design
  • Build
  • Test
sections.title: Move items between lists

sections.body: Some people can't drag, or use a screen reader on a touch screen. Give them a control that moves an item in one tap: a button or menu item inside the item with `data-ok-sortable-move-to="<list id>"` moves the item to the end of that list, in HTML and in React. For example, the **Kanban** story puts a **Move** menu on every card. Two taps also work: tap an item's handle, then a handle in another list.
sections.html: • Design
sections.title: Move items without dragging

sections.body: Disable an item to pin it, such as a summary that always comes first. A disabled item can't be dragged or grabbed, and other items never take its place: the keyboard moves them past it, and the pointer moves nothing while it is over it. In React, return `true` from `isItemDisabled`. In HTML, add `data-ok-disabled` to the item and `disabled` to its handle, so that the handle also leaves the tab order.
sections.html:
• Overview
  • Sales
  • Orders
sections.title: Keep items in place

sections.body:
By default, a moved item pushes the items between its old and its new position by one place. With the swap strategy, the moved item and the item it is dropped on trade places, and every other item stays where it is. This suits layouts where each position means something, such as the slots of a dashboard.

While people drag, or choose a target with the arrow keys, the target slides to the item's place and gets a dashed outline. Nothing changes until the item is dropped. Moving back to the item's own place cancels the swap. In React, set `strategy="swap"`: `onReorder` gets the swapped items, the same result as `arraySwap(items, from, to)`. In HTML, add `data-ok-strategy="swap"` to the list. The script swaps the two items and fires `ok:sortable:swap` first.

On touch screens, a press on an item now starts a drag instead of scrolling the page. Leave room around the items, or keep the default, in long lists that people scroll with a finger.

sections.body:
Drag events tell you where an item is while it moves, for example to show a status or to save the order only once it is dropped. They fire for the pointer, the keyboard and taps alike:

- **Start:** an item is grabbed, or a pointer drag starts.
- **Over:** the item is about to move to a new position, in its list or in another one.
- **End:** the item is dropped.
- **Cancel:** the move is cancelled, such as with Escape, before the item goes back.

In React, pass `onDragStart`, `onDragOver`, `onDragEnd` and `onDragCancel`: each gets `{ item, index, list }`, where `list` is the list's `id`. In HTML, listen for `ok:sortable:dragstart`, `ok:sortable:dragover`, `ok:sortable:dragend` and `ok:sortable:dragcancel`, whose `detail` has the item element, its index and its list element.

sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:sortable:move`** (cancelable) fires before an item moves, with `detail: { from, to, item }`.
- **`ok:sortable:swap`** (cancelable) fires before two items trade places in a list with `data-ok-strategy="swap"`, with `detail: { from, to, item, target }`. `item` is the moved item and `target` the one it is dropped on.
- **`ok:sortable:dragstart`**, **`ok:sortable:dragover`**, **`ok:sortable:dragend`** and **`ok:sortable:dragcancel`** follow a drag, with `detail: { item, index, list }`. They fire on the list that holds the item.
- **`ok:sortable:transfer`** (cancelable) fires on the list an item leaves, before the item moves to another list, with `detail: { item, from, to, index }`. `from` and `to` are the lists.
- **`ok:sortable:remove`** (cancelable) fires before an item is removed, with `detail: { index, item }`.
- **`ok:sortable:add`** fires after a new item is added from the template, with `detail: { item, index }`. Fill in its content here.
- **Instance:** `runtime.get(element, "sortable")` returns `{ move(from, to), swap(from, to), remove(index), add(), transfer(index, to, toIndex) }`. `to` is a list or its `id`. Without `toIndex`, the item goes to the end.
- **React:** `onDragStart`, `onDragOver`, `onDragEnd` and `onDragCancel` get `{ item, index, list }`. They replace the native HTML drag and drop handlers of the list element. `onReorder(items)`, `onRemove(item, index)` and `onTransfer({ item, from, to, fromIndex, index })`, where `from` and `to` are list ids. The `arrayMove(items, from, to)`, `arraySwap(items, from, to)` and `moveBetweenLists(lists, event)` helpers are exported too.

sections.body: A stepper shows progress through a sequence of steps, such as a checkout or a setup wizard. Each step has a numbered icon and a title. Steps before the active one are completed and show a check, steps after it are not reached yet. The stepper only shows progress: your app owns the active step and changes it from its Back and Next buttons. For views that people visit in any order, use **Tabs** instead.

sections.body: In React, pass `activeStep` (0-based) and change it from your buttons. Each `Step` gets its state from it: the active step, completed steps before it, not reached steps after it. Set `active`, `completed` or `disabled` on a `Step` to override the state, for example to leave a skipped step uncompleted. Once `activeStep` equals the number of steps, every step is completed. In HTML, the runtime keeps every step's state in line with `data-ok-active-step`. Buttons with `data-ok-stepper-next`, `data-ok-stepper-back` or `data-ok-stepper-reset` move the stepper they name. Back buttons are disabled on the first step.

A text field lets people enter and edit text: one line in an `<input>`, several lines in a `<textarea>`, or a choice in a `<select>`. The label sits inside the field and moves up when the field gets focus or a value. Helper text under the field gives a hint or an error message.

The field is built from native elements, so forms, autofill, the keyboard and assistive technology work as usual. It needs no JavaScript, except for growing textareas and the show-password button.

sections.body: The variant sets the field's frame. `outlined` (the default) draws a border with a gap for the label, `filled` tints the background, and `standard` draws a line under the input. Use one variant throughout a form. In HTML, only the outlined variant has the `fieldset` with the label repeated in its `legend`: that is what leaves the gap in the border.

sections.body: Pass `helperText` for a hint under the field. Set `error` to show an error: the field turns red, the input gets `aria-invalid`, and the helper text should say how to fix it. In HTML, give the helper text an `id` and point the input's `aria-describedby` at it, so screen readers read it with the field. The script sets `aria-invalid` from `data-ok-error`. Without the script, write `aria-invalid="true"` yourself.

sections.body: When the context already says what a field is for, such as a search field in a toolbar, set `hiddenLabel`. Show a placeholder instead, so sighted users know what to type. An adornment that only decorates the field can let presses through to the input: set `disablePointerEvents` on it (HTML: `data-ok-disable-pointer-events`).

sections.body: A timeline lists events in order along a vertical line, such as the steps of an order or the history of a project. Each event has a dot on the line and its content beside it. The timeline is a list (`ul`), so screen readers announce how many events it has. It needs no JavaScript.

import {
  Timeline,
  TimelineConnector,
  TimelineContent,
  TimelineDot,
  TimelineItem,
  TimelineSeparator,
} from "@owlky/react";

export function OrderHistory() {
  return (
    <Timeline>
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineSeparator>
          <TimelineDot color="success" />
          <TimelineConnector />
        </TimelineSeparator>
        <TimelineContent>Order placed</TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
      <TimelineItem>
        <TimelineSeparator>
          <TimelineDot />
        </TimelineSeparator>
        <TimelineContent>Shipped</TimelineContent>
      </TimelineItem>
    </Timeline>
  );
}

sections.body: A transfer list moves items between two lists, such as the columns you can add to a report and the ones you chose. People check items and press a move button. It is built from components you already know: each list is a **List** in a **Scrollbar**, each row a **Checkbox** with its label, and the move buttons are outlined **Buttons**. On screens under 600px the lists stack and the arrows turn to point at them.
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: In React, pass every item in `items` and the values that start on the left in `defaultLeft`. The rest start on the right. To control both sides, pass `left` and `right` and update them from `onChange(left, right)`. Moved items go to the end of the other list and are unchecked. In HTML, listen to `ok:transfer-list:change`, or read `value` on the instance.
sections.title: Read and control the sides

In HTML, `data-ok-label-count` takes a template such as `{checked} of {total}`.

sections.body: A tree view shows nested items that people expand and select, such as folders and files. It follows the WAI-ARIA tree pattern: one tab stop for the whole tree, and the arrow keys to move, open and close. `SimpleTreeView` takes `TreeItem` children. `RichTreeView` builds the same tree from data.
sections.html:
• Design
    • Wireframes
    • Mockups
    • Assets
  • Development
    • Frontend
    • Backend
sections.title: Overview

sections.body: A click on an item's row opens or closes it. Set `expansionTrigger` to `iconContainer` so only the icon does, for example when a click on the row opens a page. `defaultExpandedItems` sets the items open at first. To control them, pass `expandedItems` and `onExpandedItemsChange`. `onItemExpansionToggle` reports each toggle. Each group of child items is a Collapse: its height animates as it opens and closes, and it opens at once when the user prefers reduced motion. In HTML, keep `data-ok-collapse` on the groups.
sections.title: Expand items

sections.body: A click selects the item. Set `multiSelect` to select several: Ctrl or ⌘ click adds or removes one, and Shift click selects a range. `checkboxSelection` shows a checkbox on each item and implies `multiSelect`. Use `selectedItems` and `onSelectedItemsChange` to control the selection, or `disableSelection` when items are only for browsing.
sections.title: Select items

sections.body: By default, items with children show a chevron that turns when they open. Pass `expandIcon` and `collapseIcon` for your own pair, and `endIcon` for items without children. Set `variant` to `lines` for dashed guides beside nested items, round tinted expand icons and compact rows.
sections.title: Change the icons and the look

sections.body: With `multiSelect`, set `selectionPropagation` to `{ parents: true, descendants: true }`: selecting an item selects its descendants, and a parent is selected exactly when all its children are. `onItemSelectionToggle(itemId, isSelected)` reports each item whose selection changed, `onItemClick(itemId)` each click on a row and `onItemFocus(itemId)` each item that gets the focus. Disabled items are skipped by the arrow keys unless you set `disabledItemsFocusable`. `disableSelection` on a `TreeItem` (or `isItemSelectionDisabled` on a `RichTreeView`) keeps an item from being selected while it still expands. In HTML, write `data-ok-selection-propagation="parents descendants"` on the tree, `data-ok-disable-selection` on an item, and listen to `ok:tree-view:selectiontoggle`, `ok:tree-view:itemclick` and `ok:tree-view:itemfocus`.
sections.html:
• Design
    • Mockups
sections.title: Spread the selection and follow it

sections.body: On a `RichTreeView`, set `isItemEditable` to `true`, or to a function that picks the items. Press **F2** or double-click a label to edit it, **Enter** to save and **Escape** to cancel. Moving the focus away saves too. `onItemLabelChange(itemId, label)` reports the new label. In HTML, put `data-ok-editable` on the items (or on the tree for every item) and listen to `ok:tree-view:labelchange`: call `preventDefault()` to keep the old label.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  document.addEventListener("ok:tree-view:labelchange", (event) => {
    if (event.detail.label.trim() === "") event.preventDefault();
  });
</script>
sections.title: Edit labels

sections.body: Set `itemsReordering` on a `RichTreeView` to let people drag an item by its row. Drop it on the top or bottom edge of another row to place it before or after, or on the middle to make it a child. The keyboard does the same with **Ctrl + Shift** (**⌘ + Shift** on a Mac) and an arrow: up and down move it among its siblings, right moves it into the item above, and left moves it out of its parent. `isItemReorderable(itemId)` keeps some items in place, `canMoveItemToNewPosition` refuses a move by returning `false`, and `onItemPositionChange` reports each move with the old and new `{ parentId, index }`. In HTML, use `data-ok-items-reordering` on the tree, `data-ok-reorderable="false"` on an item, and the cancelable `ok:tree-view:move` event.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  document.addEventListener("ok:tree-view:move", (event) => {
    // Keep everything at the top level.
    if (event.detail.newPosition.parentId !== null) event.preventDefault();
  });
</script>
sections.title: Reorder items

sections.body: Pass a `dataSource` to a `RichTreeView` to load items when they are needed. `getChildrenCount(item)` tells whether an item has children: `0` for none, a number, or `-1` when you don't know yet. `getTreeItems(parentId)` returns a promise of the children, or of the root's items when `parentId` is undefined and there are no `items`. While the children load, the item shows a progress indicator and is marked `aria-busy`. If loading fails, the item shows the error and loads again when it is expanded again. In HTML, mark the items with `data-ok-lazy` and an empty group, and pass the data source to the instance's `setDataSource()`: its items are `{ id, label, childrenCount }` and are built as text.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const tree = document.querySelector("[data-ok-tree-view]");
  Owlky.runtime.get(tree, "tree-view").setDataSource({
    getTreeItems: (parentId) => fetch(`/api/folders?parent=${parentId ?? ""}`).then((response) => response.json()),
  });
</script>
sections.title: Load children on demand

sections.body: Pass a ref from `useTreeViewApiRef()` as `apiRef` to control the tree from your code. `expandAll()`, `collapseAll()`, `expandToDepth(depth)` and `expandSubtree(itemId)` open many items at once, and `focusItem`, `selectItem`, `setItemExpansion`, `getItem`, `getItemTree` and `setEditedItem` work on one. Set `highlight` to a search text: matching labels are marked and their ancestors' labels are bold, so people see where the matches are. In HTML, the instance has the same expansion methods, and `data-ok-highlight` or `highlight(query)` marks the matches.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const tree = document.querySelector("[data-ok-tree-view]");
  const instance = Owlky.runtime.get(tree, "tree-view");
  instance.expandToDepth(2);
  document.querySelector("#tree-search").addEventListener("input", (event) => {
    instance.highlight(event.target.value);
  });
</script>
sections.title: Expand everything and highlight matches

sections.title: Options

sections.body: These props set the items and the state. They aren't options, because HTML writes them as markup.
sections.title: Content and behavior

sections.body:
- **`ok:tree-view:expand`** (cancelable) fires on the tree with `detail.itemId` and `detail.expanded`.
- **`ok:tree-view:select`** (cancelable) fires with `detail.selectedItems`.
- **`ok:tree-view:selectiontoggle`** fires once per item whose selection changed, with `detail.itemId` and `detail.selected`. **`ok:tree-view:itemclick`** and **`ok:tree-view:itemfocus`** fire with `detail.itemId`.
- **`ok:tree-view:labelchange`** (cancelable) fires before an edited label is saved, with `detail.itemId` and `detail.label`.
- **`ok:tree-view:move`** (cancelable) fires before an item moves, and **`ok:tree-view:positionchange`** after it, with `detail.itemId`, `detail.oldPosition` and `detail.newPosition`.

sections.body: An upload lets people choose files by dropping them on a zone, by pressing the zone to open the file dialog, or by pasting them. It checks each file against the types, sizes and counts you allow, lists the files it keeps with a preview, a name and a size, and lists the rejected files with the reasons. The zone is built around a native file input, so it works with the keyboard and screen readers, and a form submits the files it holds. The upload never sends files anywhere: you decide when and how to send them.

sections.body: Turn on `multiple` to keep adding files: each drop or pick adds its files to the list. Without it, a new file replaces the current one. In HTML, put `multiple` on the input and add the list, its item `<template>` and, if you want them, the **Remove all** and **Upload** buttons. In React, `onRemoveAll` and `onUpload` show those buttons. Pass `value` with `onChange` to control the files yourself; `onChange` receives every file the upload holds.

The file dialog shows those types, and dropped or pasted files are checked against them too. `maxSize` and `minSize` are in bytes. `maxFiles` caps how many files a multiple upload holds. Add your own check with `validator`: it receives each file and returns `null`, an error `{ code, message }` or a list of errors, and it may return a promise. Rejected files appear under the zone with their reasons. Rewrite the messages, for example to translate them, with `getErrorMessage`.

sections.body: The upload copies the files it holds into its input, so a form with the input's `name` submits them, including dropped and pasted files. To send them yourself, read `files` from the HTML instance or the `onChange` value in React, and post them with `fetch()` and `FormData`. The **Upload** button gives you the files in `onUpload` (HTML: the `ok:upload:upload` event). Files a user chose before, such as a saved avatar, can be URL strings in `value`: the upload shows them but can't put them in the input.

sections.body: While files are over the zone, the browser tells only their types and their count. `dragFileRejections` lists the dragged files that would be rejected, each with its `index`, `type` and `errors` (`file-invalid-type` or `too-many-files`), so the zone can say why before the drop. In React, read it from the state that `placeholder` receives, or from `useDropzone`. In HTML, read `detail.rejections` of the `ok:upload:drag` event, or the instance's `dragState.rejections`. File names and sizes are only known at drop time, so the other checks run then.

sections.body: In React, `useDropzone(options)` gives the upload's behavior without its look: spread `getRootProps()` on your drop target and `getInputProps()` on a file input inside it. The root opens the file dialog on a press, Enter or Space, takes dropped and pasted files, and reports them to `onDrop(accepted, rejections)`. The hook returns the same drag state as the zone (`isDragActive`, `isDragAccept`, `isDragReject`, `dragFileRejections`), plus `isFocused`, `acceptedFiles`, `fileRejections` and `open()`. `Dropzone` is the same hook as a component that takes a render function. Give the root a name and a role, as in the example: the input is hidden, so the root is the control people reach. In HTML, the `upload` runtime is the behavior, and `createUploadController` from `@owlky/core` drives markup of your own.

sections.body: A walktour guides people through a page, one step at a time. Each step is a small dialog next to the element it explains. An overlay dims the rest of the page and leaves a spotlight on that element. People move on with **Next**, go back with **Back**, end the tour with **Skip**, and close a step with the close button or Escape. A progress bar and a step count show how far they are. Instead of opening a step at once, a tour can show a pulsing beacon on the element, which people select when they are ready.

sections.title: Overview

sections.body: In React, pass the steps as data. Each step has a `target`, which is a CSS selector, an element, a ref or a function that returns the element. It also has its `content` and, usually, a `title` that names the dialog. `placement` puts the step on a side of the target, such as `bottom` or `left-start`. Use `auto` to pick the side with the most room, or `center` for a step in the middle of the screen with no target. A step can override most options of the tour, such as `disableBeacon`, `spotlightClicks` or `showSkipButton`. In HTML, write one step element per step. `data-ok-target` holds the selector, and an option attribute on a step overrides the tour's. The value `false` turns a tour option off for that step.

sections.body: The tour runs while `run` is `true`. Setting it to `false` pauses the tour, and setting it back resumes it. A tour that finished or was skipped starts over. `apiRef` gives you `start`, `stop`, `reset`, `next`, `prev`, `go`, `close`, `skip` and `open`. To control the current step yourself, pass `stepIndex` and update it from `onStepChange`. In HTML, `data-ok-run` runs the tour, a button with `data-ok-walktour-start` starts it over, and the instance has the same methods.

<button type="button" data-ok-button data-ok-walktour-start="tour" data-ok-index="0">Start the tour</button>

<script type="module">
  // Or from code, once the runtime has started.
  const tour = window.Owlky.get(document.getElementById("tour"), "walktour");
  tour.start();
  tour.go(2);
</script>

sections.body: Without `continuous`, the primary button reads **Close**: it closes the step and shows a beacon on the next target. People select the beacon to open that step. In a continuous tour, **Next** and **Back** go from step to step without beacons, and closing a step with the close button, Escape or the overlay shows the next step's beacon. `disableBeacon` opens steps at once, for the whole tour or for one step.

sections.body: The overlay blocks the page while a step is open, so the step is a modal dialog. `spotlightClicks` lets people use the element in the spotlight, and `disableOverlay` removes the overlay: in both cases the step is no longer modal. `disableOverlayClose` keeps a click on the overlay from closing the step. `spotlightPadding` sets the space around the target and `spotlightRadius` the spotlight's corners, in pixels. When a target is out of view, the tour scrolls it into view and keeps `scrollOffset` pixels above it. `disableScrolling` turns that off, and `scrollToFirstStep` scrolls for the first step too.

sections.body: A step can point at an element that isn't on the page yet, such as an item in a closed menu. `before` runs when the step is about to show, before the tour looks for its target. Return a promise, and the tour waits for it before it shows the step, for up to `beforeTimeout` milliseconds (5000 by default, `0` for no limit). If the promise rejects or takes too long, the tour reports an `error` event and goes on. `after` runs once the step has ended, for example to close the menu again. The tour doesn't wait for it. Set both on the tour for every step, or on a step for that step only. In HTML, listen for `ok:walktour:beforestep` and pass a promise to `event.detail.waitUntil()`. For `after`, listen for the `step:after` event. The step that ends always reports `step:after` before the next step's `before` runs.
sections.html:
<script type="module">
  const root = document.getElementById("tour");
  const menu = document.getElementById("menu");
  root.addEventListener("ok:walktour:beforestep", (event) => {
    // Step 2 points at an item in the menu: open the menu and wait for its animation.
    if (event.detail.index === 1) {
      menu.hidden = false;
      event.detail.waitUntil(new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 300)));
    }
  });
  root.addEventListener("ok:walktour:event", (event) => {
    if (event.detail.type === "step:after" && event.detail.index === 1) menu.hidden = true;
  });
</script>
sections.title: Run code before and after a step

sections.body: A step whose target isn't on the page yet waits for it for `targetWaitTimeout` milliseconds, 1000 by default. The tour looks for the target every 100 milliseconds and shows the step as soon as it appears, such as after a route change or a lazy load. If the target doesn't come, the step is skipped with an `error:target-not-found` event. Set `targetWaitTimeout` to `0` to skip such steps at once. Nothing shows while the tour waits, and the tour's `state.waiting` is `true`.

sections.title: Wait for targets

sections.body: By default, a step scrolls its target into view and puts it in the spotlight. `scrollTarget` scrolls to another element instead, such as the section a small button sits in. `spotlightTarget` highlights another element instead, such as the whole card around a button. The tooltip and the beacon stay on the target. Scrolling takes `scrollDuration` milliseconds, 300 by default, and is instant at `0` or when the system asks for reduced motion. A target that doesn't move when the page scrolls, such as a fixed header, isn't scrolled to. The tour finds fixed elements on its own, and `isFixed` marks a target that it can't detect. In HTML, `data-ok-scroll-target` and `data-ok-spotlight-target` take CSS selectors.

With `hover`, the step opens as soon as a mouse moves over the beacon, while keyboard and touch users still select it. `beaconPlacement` puts the beacon on another side of the target than the tooltip, such as `left` for a tooltip at the `bottom`. `closeButtonAction` sets what the close button does: `close` closes the step and shows the next step's beacon, and `skip` ends the tour, like **Skip**. All three can be set on the tour or on one step.

sections.body: React reports changes with `onStepChange(index, details)`, `onStatusChange(status, details)` and `onEvent(type, data)`. `onEvent` receives every event of the tour in order: `tour:start`, `step:before-hook`, `step:before`, `beacon`, `tooltip`, `step:after`, `step:after-hook`, `tour:end`, `tour:status`, `error:target-not-found` and `error`. Each comes with the action, the control that asked for it, the step, the status and the number of steps, and `error` events also carry the `error`. In HTML, listen for `ok:walktour:change` (the new state), `ok:walktour:event` (the same events as `onEvent`), `ok:walktour:beforestep` (a step is about to show) and `ok:walktour:beforechange`, which you can cancel to keep the current step. A step whose target doesn't appear in time is skipped.

sections.body:
- Each step is a dialog named by its title (or "Step 2 of 5" without one) and described by its content. While the overlay blocks the page, the step is modal: Tab stays inside it and the rest of the page is inert.
- `disableFocusTrap` lets Tab leave the step. The step is then no longer modal, so screen readers can reach the page too. Use it when the step asks people to use something outside it.
- `beaconTrigger="hover"` only adds a way to open a step: keyboard and touch users still select the beacon.
- Focus moves to the step's primary button when a step opens, to the beacon when a step closes to one, and back to where it was when the tour ends.
- A polite live region announces "Step 2 of 5" when a step opens.
- The beacon is a button named "Open the dialog". Change the text with `locale.open`.
- Escape closes a step unless `disableCloseOnEsc` is set. Keep it on: it is the quickest way out for keyboard users.
- The beacon's pulse stops when the system asks for reduced motion, and scrolling to a target is instant then.
